## Can an “AI command line” replace the GUI as the primary user experience for computers, assuming the technology improves and irrespective of today’s state?

*https://www.quora.com/Can-an-AI-command-line-replace-the-GUI-as-the-primary-user-experience-for-computers-assuming-the-technology-improves-and-irrespective-of-today-s-state/answer/Alan-Kay-11*

The “related questions” have interesting slants — some of which make more or less sense.

I think most people should be able to answer this for themselves if they look at this from a number of different angles.

One is that we have multiple ways of “perceiving”, “knowing”, “learning”, etc. — for example by touch, sound, vision, symbolic representations, abstract languagues, etc. Besides inventing interactive computer graphics, Ivan Sutherland pointed out (in a famous 1964 paper) that “the ultimate display” should be able to do every kind of I/O that humans can do and experience. His famous last line with typical Ivan humor was “In the ultimate display, a simulated bullet would be fatal to its operator”!

One of the inventors of Cognitive Psychology — Jerome Bruner — explored three of our ways of knowing — tactile/kinesthetic, configural (vision, audio), symbolic — in his ideas about learning and teaching, and we used these as a basis for thinking about UI at Parc (we didn’t call it Graphical UI, just UI, etc.).

All kinds of “command lines” (whether “AI” or not) assume the users know what they want and more or less how to ask for it. This doesn’t cover enough ground for the entire user experience — so if the user is confined just to this mode, many things that might be good for them might be missed (even if the “AI” is good). This is the bug with Google and with slaves/assistants/etc. You are limited by what you know — and most people don’t know much/enough.

A good UI is much more than a command environment, it also needs to teach in various ways, it needs to be safely explorable in many ways, etc.

Let’s just look at the latter for a few minutes. Safely explorable implies that a comprehensive UNDO at all levels has been implemented. I’ve been conducting experiments for several years that reveal most users of smart phones don’t know how to invoke UNDO (and in fact Siri, etc. doesn’t know), and the few who do, don’t know how to invoke UNDO on an iPad. And the iPad won’t tell us.

In fact, UNDO has been deemphasized in UIs generally (I think partly becuase most of today’s programmers are not up to including it (technically and morally), and because most programming languages have no provision for it because they are terribly low-level for most needs today), etc. Yikes!

Even if Siri did know how to invoke UNDO and could even do it for you, most users would still not be aware of it unless they were told somehow. (This brings up the problem of “hidden useful features” and how to let the user know about them — the UI also needs to deal with the “forgetting problem”, etc.)

When I try to explain something to someone — whether human or “AI” — I often resort to a great invention from 40,000 years ago: pictures and drawings as part of a description. (Newton used these to great effect in the Principia, (one of the most important books ever written, and not a “command line book”, etc.)

I’m using “etc.” over and over to try to make the point that most of this should be completely obvious to any computerist (and most users/readers).

But it isn’t, and mostly because of one of the many bugs in our all too human feeble attempts to navigate through the world. One of the simplest — and worst — manifestations of this is to choose a tiny subset of the world to live in, and then to insist that it is the world. Computerists have been particularly prone to this over the years in many areas, including programming styles and languages, UIs, what users need, what “AI” actually means, the consequences of stupid/ignorant people doing stupid/ignorant and dangerous implementations, etc., etc.

Note that “ignorance” closely resembles “stupidity” …

Just because any idea seems to be “successful” doesn’t at all imply that it is good (our species has propagated any number of really bad ideas for hundreds of thousands of years, not just hundreds of years or decades).

I would hope that any UI in the future would allow a user to ask for what they want if they know it, and that the larger UI enviroment would be doing its best to teach the user more about the world and more about what would be good for them, and to show them, etc.

Finally, we have to ask “How much help is too much help?”.

Do we really want to replace everything that is good for a person to do, with a slave to do it for us? A prosthetic on a healthy limb will atrophy the limb. A prosthetic on a mind with atrophy the mind. (That is what has been happening for quite a bit longer than “AI” or “UIs” or “GUIs” have been around — but scaling up human stupidity/ignorance with the industrial revolution is a new kind of disaster for our weak minded species.)

Etc. Etc. …

## Did Alan Kay know Bill Atkinson? Was there any cross-fertilization between SmallTalk and HyperCard/Talk?

*https://www.quora.com/Did-Alan-Kay-know-Bill-Atkinson-Was-there-any-cross-fertilization-between-SmallTalk-and-HyperCard-Talk/answer/Alan-Kay-11*

I first met Bill at the famous Steve Jobs visit to Parc to see the Smalltalk system, its GUI, etc. (I might have run into him earlier). After a stint at Atari, Steve Jobs hired me in 1984 as an Apple Fellow (Butler and I had been made Fellows towards the end of our stay at Xerox). Bill had been made an Apple Fellow for his many contributions, especially to the Lisa and Macintosh projects. He was very talented and creative, etc. and our relationship could be characterized as “brotherly”.

Fellows in most organizations are both autonomous and have access to a research stipend that allows research projects of a few people to be started without needing signoff from management.

Bill liked the “Dynabook” idea and his slant on it was that what you saw on the screen was a particular “card” of an unlimited number that you could find, link to, etc. He called the machine “Magic Slate” and the SW part “Wild Card”. He did a subset of this as a Mac “accessory” called “Rolodex”, and I thought it was the neatest greatest little thing I’d seen on a personal computer. Part of Bill’s genius was in “small things done wonderfully”, and this was an example.

He and his little group made a larger vesion with more capabilities (roughly what came to be known as “Hypercard level 4”) — basically most things but leaving out scripting.

One day Bill came to me in tears. He had just been turned down by Apple Product when he tried to get them to develop and ship “Wild Card” on Macs.

I was friendly with John Sculley, and said let’s get John to see this. John liked it and then said after finding out about the turn-down, “I’ll push this through”. (This made me realize that Apple was in a bit of trouble: a CEO should never have to be the Champion of a product in a company that is running correctly.)

I said to John, when you do this, make sure that this can be scripted: this is the main thing it lacks right now.

I realized that I didn’t have the particular “end-user sensibility” that Bill had, and decided not to butt in regarding the design of the scripting (and I was right: I would have ruined the naive charm of Hypertalk). They found Dan Winkler to be the main designer of the scripting part, and he and his team did a great job that didn’t break the charm and feel of the original idea.

Another key player was Carol Kaehler, who designed much of the surrounding “user amenities” and did most of the “Help Stack”.

Because Sculley was driving it, the development effort was very well funded and was the best overall example I’d seen of developing a product from a research prototype.

Hypercard (there was a trademark conflict with the original name) was not just an instant success, but in a few years Apple was able to identify at least 4 million creators of new HyperApps — making it the most successful programming system in history.

I regarded it as a breakthrough for the “persons” who used “personal computers” in that it gave the first glimpse of the many things that needed to not just be done well, but done well in the psychic space of actual end-users.

Smalltalk had very little influence on Hypercard — besides its influence on the Mac — and vice versa. However, Hypercard had a great influence on the Etoys system our group did later at Disney, which was an attempt to make a system for children that combined what was great about Hypercard, Smalltalk, Star Logo, etc., (and to eliminate what was not so good for end-users). This wound up working really well, and it would not have been as good without Hypercard having been done.

Apple the company — and Steve, the returned “saviour” for Apple — did not understand the Internet, and that Hypercard was a fantastic model for a truly great browser. Instead, it was brushed aside and much more mundane ideas — pretty much everywhere in the general business — ruled to the eventual detriment of most end-users today.

## What role did the unique features of the Alto computer play in the development of programming languages like Smalltalk and Lisp?

*https://www.quora.com/What-role-did-the-unique-features-of-the-Alto-computer-play-in-the-development-of-programming-languages-like-Smalltalk-and-Lisp/answer/Alan-Kay-11*

I realized that I was being unjustifiably harsh in my first paragraph (now the 2nd) below. It is actually a more reasonable question than as I initially interpreted it. The unique features of the Alto did play a part in the development of Smalltalk in part because the special features were put in the Alto because we knew they would help in our (and the rest of Parc’s) VHLL research efforts. In sum: (a) we knew “sort of” how things were going to go, but did not yet have the details that would make a pure HW design possible, and (b) we needed to be able to make at least 100 machines, and a pure HW version, even if we knew all the answers would be too expensive per unit. One of my slogans back then was “HW is just SW crystallized early”, and the ratios of costs and capacities indicated that a “meta-machine” using Wilkes’ invention of microcode — and making it dynamically loadable — would be a very good tradeoff. This approach was not controversial in the Parc research community, even though it remained so outside.

The simplest and most important part of the answer is that the question is exactly backwards — in the sense that the Alto was explicitly designed to be a good foundation for Very High Level Languages such as Lisp (implemented ca 1959) and Smalltalk (the earliest working version predated the Alto).

This should make some sense when contemplated. The only reason for a programmable computer is to run programs, and being able to invent HLLs and VHLLs to make it easier to write programs would greatly facilitate the whole process. The problem was that things had started out with HW that programmers were supposed to then use. It was most generally the case that powerful ideas in software organization very often didn’t find the features in existing hardware, and emulating them in SW sometimes resulted in too inefficient results.

A real forcing function was provided by Algol and a solution was the Burroughs B5000 (main designer Bob Barton) which was hardware that matched up to what was important to the language (and also to what was being learned about scaling and complex systems). I have written other Quora answers about this machine.

Even newer ideas again put a strain on the B5000, and it was realized by the mid-60s or so that a much better approach would be to make a “meta-machine” where the invention of microcode by Maurice Wilkes could be exploited. The basic approach here was to exploit the difference in speeds between core memory RAM and faster more expensive ways to make smaller memories and simple processors. The idea to visualize is that if the inner machine was always waiting on core to cycle then what it was doing couldn’t be done faster with straight logic, and therefore you were emulating logic without losing overall throughput.

So you not only could simulate any architecture, but — if the microcode memory was dynamically loadable — you could incorporate new understandings of process description simply by writing new microcode, and you would — in effect — be creating the “HW” on the fly that your new SW ideas required.

The Alto didn’t originate these ideas, but it was one of the earliest to put all of the elements together in a practical fashion. Part of the reason we could build so many Altos, was that the microcode could also emulate what was normally HW, and thus reduce the overall costs of building many machines (we wound up building about 2000 of them).

So the process was to think about advances in language semantics, ask questions about representations, and then create the machine architecture well suited to these via microcoding. All the VHLLs we used at Parc had their own custom microcode that defined the kernal “HW” in the form of a SW virtual machine. When you started up e.g. Lisp or Smalltalk, what got loaded first was the microcode that defined the particular virtual machine, etc.

All the computers we built at Parc used this idea. This meant that only a few thousand lines of code were needed to allow any of these machines to run any of the SW environments we were experimenting with.

## How much did Daniel Bobrow and Alan Kay interact at PARC in the days that led to the invention of modern Object-Oriented Programming? Is Bobrow and Winograd's "An Overview of KRL" (1976) the first publication using OO in its modern meaning?

*https://www.quora.com/How-much-did-Daniel-Bobrow-and-Alan-Kay-interact-at-PARC-in-the-days-that-led-to-the-invention-of-modern-Object-Oriented-Programming-Is-Bobrow-and-Winograds-An-Overview-of-KRL-1976-the-first-publication-using-OO-in/answer/Alan-Kay-11*

Danny and I were friends from the time I first met him (he a researcher from MIT now at BBN) and I was a first year grad student (this was probably in 1967).

He was a very friendly guy and was both interested in AI (meaning AGI back then) and programming language ideas — he was one of many such ARPA researchers who bounced ideas off each other. We were all overjoyed a few years later when Parc started up and he joined the three ring circus there.

We continued our friendship, tennis competitions, and talk about language architectures. Danny was a very helpful editor and critic on my first public Dynabook paper (ACM Nat’l Convention 1972).

One of the most interesting and best uses of Smalltalk at Parc was as the implementation vehicle for the PIE system by Danny Bobrow and Ira Goldstein. This advanced several concepts of OO and of temporal tagging, etc.

I don’t know what the first publication to use OO in its modern meaning (I’m a bit afraid to ask what this might mean), but it would have happened way before 1976.

## Has anyone without a professional background in engineering, science, mathematics, etc. ever invented something solely based on a great idea?

*https://www.quora.com/Has-anyone-without-a-professional-background-in-engineering-science-mathematics-etc-ever-invented-something-solely-based-on-a-great-idea/answer/Alan-Kay-11*

There are already lots of good answers to this, so I’ll just add a larger observation made by the philosopher/mathematician Albert North Whitehead: “The main invention of the 19th century was Invention itself”.

He pointed to the immense boom in “letters patent” in Great Britain to show that almost everyone seemed to be inventing: as though it was in the air. It was a topic of conversation at parties, etc.

The detailed history of how a few key inventions that started the industrial revolution also made it “a thing” to invent something is too long for Quora. But you can easily find books on many actually crazy inventions that were patented: one that comes to mind is a hat that would tip itself to a lady if you moved your head correctly!

## How long have you been designing a computer system?

*https://www.quora.com/How-long-have-you-been-designing-a-computer-system/answer/Alan-Kay-11*

I started “coding as a real job” in the US Air Force in 1962. In those days “coding” and “programming” had rather different meanings. “Coding” was essentially being a human compiler to turn designs (mostly in terms of flow charts) into working machine code by way of writing in an assembly language. Some of the assemblers we used — such as IBM Autocoder — had fairly powerful abilities to construct macros, so design started to creep into one’s coding skills.

“Programming” included the design of algorithms and systems.

Most coders started doing some design soon after writing their first programs. One of the first real systems designs I did was a complex scheme for merge sorting with very slow tape drives, which was likely done around the end of 1962 or beginning of 1963.

So the answer is about 63 years …

## I have heard so many amazing stories of PARC where innovation was driven by the creativity and curiosity of the developers. Does this type of scenario exist anywhere in today's software industry?

*https://www.quora.com/I-have-heard-so-many-amazing-stories-of-PARC-where-innovation-was-driven-by-the-creativity-and-curiosity-of-the-developers-Does-this-type-of-scenario-exist-anywhere-in-todays-software-industry/answer/Alan-Kay-11*

In the early ‘80s Regis McKenna, one of the shapers of the Silicon Valley culture, clarified terms by pointing out that “invention” was what places like Xerox Parc did, and “innovation” was what companies like Apple did. The latter takes much more work and funding than the former, but doesn’t help anyone without a hefty admixture of “invention”.

Despite the smaller costs of real invention — and the incredible ROIs from the successes — most of the best funding diminished to below critical masses in the ’80s and is still quite non-existent (as far as I can tell). For example, just the profits from the invention of laser printing at Parc paid for the entire cost of Parc over the first 10 or so years (its most productive period) by roughly a factor of 200. The entire output of Parc constituted the invention of an entire new industry.

Another nitpick with terminology: it would be most appropriate to call the people at Xerox Parc “researchers” rather than “developers”.

I am aware of a number of “working group” sized organizations today whose process and level of researchers — both creatively and technically — are comparable to Parc. In the not too distant past I was part of one of these (Viewpoints Research Institute). Two of several really interesting ones today are Ink And Switch (James Lindenbaum) and DynamicLand (by Bret Victor). They are both “vision-based” and have been willing and able to “problem find” rather than to just try to make something that can be sold.

They are doing good things — and real research — but my experience whispers that they need to be part of a larger research institution to be as effective as e.g. Parc.

Parc was an organization “the next size larger” so it had quite a few “working group” sized activities. Looking back, I think this was critical — and critical even beyond the imagination of Bob Taylor, who did so much to shape the culture at Parc. We found out after the Parc diaspora in the 80s when the views of Xerox and of the researchers diverged to the point of break up. The “working groups” found homes in the 80s, but the synergies from the larger situation at Parc no longer provided the “secret sauce” that made it really special. (Something similar happened — on an even larger scale — during the “divestiture period” of ATT which eventually dissolved Bell Labs.)

Interesting facts are that the cost (and headcount) of Xerox Parc were still quite small, but there was definitely a “Goldilocks” factor in what actually constituted a critical mass of people and ideas. The nature of the funding (and funders) that made the ARPA/Parc research community possible no longer exists anywhere in the world as far as I can tell.

## Could you critique my short essay about “the computer as a medium” (Amiga → Smalltalk) and tell me what doesn’t hold up?

*https://www.quora.com/Could-you-critique-my-short-essay-about-the-computer-as-a-medium-Amiga-Smalltalk-and-tell-me-what-doesn-t-hold-up/answer/Alan-Kay-11*

I don’t have a link to this essay — or did I miss something?

Added 12 Feb 2026

Please forgive me in advance for only working from a machine translation of your article.

The first thing to keep in mind for anyone attempting an historical account is that the complex past at the very least needs to be thought about in terms of parallel, often intersecting, threads, whereas narrative (writing) is a single dimensional medium. This enormous difference has to be addressed in one way or another.

For example, most histories don’t reflect the parallel threads by supplying a simple 2+D map showing the main threads (the “+” is because the threads may have to overlap in some cases). A map would help this article.

Also extreme care in clarity in the early parts will help greatly.

For example, your title (translated to English) is

“When the computer was a medium - From Amiga to Smalltalk”

This seems to be an historical statement, but it misleads — it is actually your personal journey — which started with your encounter with a computer created in the 80s and then wound up with meeting a software system invented about 15 years earlier.

I would suggest that the second part be changed to — from the Amiga back to Smalltalk. This more accurately reflects what you describe in your article, and also helps the reader.

In fact, part of what you like about the Amiga is the overlapping windows and pointing UI, and the theory behind the look and feel, and these were derived from the Parc GUI which originated in Smalltalk.

Most histories of events to which I was actually present are not very accurate — with inaccuracies both small and large. Nitpicking these errors made by well-meaning authors is a bit beside the point if the larger article conveys an important idea. I think you succeed in the large here, and that the article makes a positive contribution.

But, since you asked me to critique it: just for the record …

My thoughts about media mostly came in the 196os from grappling with understanding Marshall McLuhan (who had many of the most important insights about media). My little addition was to notice that — since the computer could simulate anything that could be described — it was a true metamedium, and that meant there were likely media on the computer that could only exist because of the computer.

I think I would point out that the Alto at Parc could do excellent versions of real-time: graphics, animation, sound, music, multitasking, and programming coexisting together. My much later comment on the Amiga was because I thought it was the first and most successful consumer level project in the 80s to be able to do what our research machine in the 70s had pioneered.

Atari could have made something of its early investment/loan in the Amiga project (IIRC I think it was about $500K) when Atari got in trouble and needed new product to bail out.

By the way “Ted Hoff” was the inventor of the first onchip CPU (the Intel 4004). he and I were good friends, and shared an office while at Atari.

“The conceptual conection” between Smalltalk and the Amiga can be traced back to the 1950s, and especially to the ARPA computer research community. There were many important systems that had the same feel that predated Smalltalk.

Many of the things that made Smalltalk feel special were due to my partner in crime at Parc: Dan Ingalls. What you like about Smalltalk was due to an entire group happily working together.

I think this is more than you asked for, and almost certainly more than most readers would wish.

Best wishes

Alan

## If you brought back Alan Turing, John von Neumann, and Claude Shannon today and gave them 10 years to learn modern science, would they still revolutionize AI and cloud computing?

*https://www.quora.com/If-you-brought-back-Alan-Turing-John-von-Neumann-and-Claude-Shannon-today-and-gave-them-10-years-to-learn-modern-science-would-they-still-revolutionize-AI-and-cloud-computing/answer/Alan-Kay-11*

Genius is genius in any age. Effective genius has to do with raw capacity, inner sense of style, and the era in which they live.

One answer to the question is that all three of these would be considered geniuses today. They would not necessarily be as effective — they might be less, or even more so — in today’s situations.

I’m answering like this because there are super high talents in every age, but there’s a sense in which the age singles out the talents that will be most effective for that age. I’m thinking of many situations in the 60s when the scarcity of resources combined with high ideals “found” researchers who could deal brilliantly with the combination. Our age would no doubt single out researchers with a feel for large scales.

In many cases — some would be as “effectively genius” in any age (I’m thinking of someone like Butler Lampson …).

## What do you think of Rob Pike's assertion that "data structures, not algorithms, are central to programming"?

*https://www.quora.com/What-do-you-think-of-Rob-Pikes-assertion-that-data-structures-not-algorithms-are-central-to-programming/answer/Alan-Kay-11*

Looking at some of the other answers will be worthwhile. (Alon Amit provides more context.)

Before I try to answer this, let me ask those who are willing to comment what they see as the immense deadly flaw in this perspective? (Please comment rather than upvoting at this point!)

Added Jan 20th 2026 — OK. I mentioned before that I don’t like to write criticisms because they seem to morally require much more substantive detail than short praise. Here, we have a name attached to a question, but we don’t really know the context (or even whether this is what that person actually said). So I propose here to look at the Amit version of this as an isolated utterance, and react to it.

Data dominates. If you've chosen the right data structures and organized things well, the algorithms will almost always be self-evident. Data structures, not algorithms, are central to programming.

If we are talking about computing in general, this is an example of “category confusion” — likely with simple marking media such as paper, and not with computers at all. However, we could also say that the category confusion is deeper than that, and is with *programming* or even *meaning* itself.

We can also squint at this from another angle with the observation that in much of computer over history *pragmatics have dominated semantics (including often obliterating the latter)*.

Or we can note that we have nothing — for markings — with humans or computers — if we don’t have process …

If we take a simple marking — such as sine(x) — we have a certain meaningful mathematical relationship in mind that our representations and uses of in computing want to not lose touch with. If we have an “x” in mind, then we want whatever this is to give us a number representation that is close enough to the mathematical meaning for our purposes and intentions. Note that in a computer language it doesn’t matter whether this is always internally represented by a pattern of bits: there is a process (generated by a program) whether we think of this as “data” (it could be a table), or “program” (there are programs that can generate approximations of sine(x)). It could be a mixture (an array for integer degrees and a program to compute the rest). In any case, “data” is not fundamental.

In a more “data-base-case”, let’s consider the query (notice that “sine(x)” could be considered a query) date-of-birth(Bob). Here we might be using this “base” as a way to store and retrieve *properties* of *things*. The category confusion here (which was swept under the rug of pragmatics) is that “age-of” is also a *property* of a thing. In both cases we are semantically dealing with a property and we expect a number of some kind as the functional association with the property and the thing/person mentioned.

Note that not only do we need “age-of(Bob)” to be computed at the time of the query (from date-of-birth(Bob) and current-time, but we should ask the question of whether we want the “retrieval” to be a mere number. The mere number will eventually lose its meaning.

Maybe the result of the “retrieval” should be a process that will always try to mean “age-of(Bob)”. Note that this could be considered a “type” (and it would be really valuable to have such types) but that this is far beyond most conceptions of types after 80 years of programming computers.

Are we going to (a) ignore this? (b) have special purpose patches of code? (c) or meet it straight on and see that “data as organization of bits” is too weak an idea to survive the earliest historical needs for computing.

Intel might not yet understand this — etc — but *computing needs to*. The Alto at Parc didn’t have floating point hardware. Smalltalk at Parc did have many kinds of numbers and would — behind the scenes — compute the meaning (and convert automatically) when necessary (if a primitive failed to be found in the HW). This was because “humans think first in terms of magnitudes” (and we can deal with the many ways of representing and computing these as mostly invisible optimizations).

A key idea here is: we are always computing even when we just might think we are “using” a “data structure” — something has to run according to a scheme in order to “do” or “use” anything. Once this is grasped, then it can be turned to our great advantage to start recapturing semantics in ways that “mere marking media” can’t (note what “meaning” implies if a human comes upon a marked up paper… — “something has to run according to a scheme …”).

How about as a slogan: The center of programming is *meaning* ?

I generally write too long for Quora, so I’ll pause here. There is much more that can be said in large terms about “conceptions of what computing is, especially within the field — and how this can impede or aid progress in both thinking and tools”.

This is one of those “Point of view is worth 80 IQ points” issues (and where the sign bit can be “+” or “-”.

## Mr. Alan Kay. You’ve said Smalltalk was about messages, not objects, and about creating a medium for thought. Do you think modern software has lost that goal—and is it still possible today to build systems that truly support human thinking?

*https://www.quora.com/Mr-Alan-Kay-You-ve-said-Smalltalk-was-about-messages-not-objects-and-about-creating-a-medium-for-thought-Do-you-think-modern-software-has-lost-that-goal-and-is-it-still-possible-today-to-build-systems-that-truly/answer/Alan-Kay-11*

This is several questions—which don’t have a strong overlap.

The “messages” part — and for programming techniques in general — can largely be summed up by the (oversimplification): There has been no corrresponding “Moore’s Law” for software development and systems. We have seen factors of billions (even trillions) of scale in capacity and elementary computing speeds. By contrast, not much has happened—especially with regard to *engineering* considerations—since the 1980s. (I am struggling to avoid a too long screed here!)

Much can be achieved by trying to discard present views and simply look at the engineering demands (and dangers to human life) brought by scalings. A thought as simple as “Anyone can make a doghouse which will not fall in on the dog, but trying to scale most methods by only a factor of 100 will be very dangerous—even fatal—for the dog” can help start thinking off in a much better direction.

By its nature making things with materials *is* also a medium for thought. The problem is that the qualifying adjective is missing. Since “most ideas are mediocre down to bad” just making is not likely to produce thoughts that help produce better worlds (and usually the opposite!).

The ideals of the 60s were to shape things so that human thought was qualitatively improved in important ways. I still think that it is possible, but it is very likely that—as Montessori pointed out at the beginning of the 20th century—most humans aren’t able to learn “epistemology in a classroom” (most learn their outlook on knowledge, how to find and vet it, whether to believe or test, etc. from growing up in a culture with its outlook manifested *in* the culture). Montessori’s insight was that therefore the form of schools—not so much its courses, etc.—had to *be a culture* that embodied the best ways to think, and presented to the children as a culture (not a syllabus).

In a school with this kind of thinking—that has chosen science as one of its facets for outlook—computers can really help if used *very very* carefully. This has many parallels to the pitfalls of trying to use books to help children learn science. First and foremost, science is about the relationship (and negotiations) between the external world (which produces phenomena) and our internal worlds (which assign meanings and beliefs to what we think the phenoman signifies). We can understand why it is so difficult to learn real science (and why it took so long to even discover it) by contemplating just how close to solipsism are our brain/minds, and why there are so many notions about us and the external world.

My favorite Einstein quote (to the Prussian Academy of Sciences, January 27, 1921) was: " ... as far as the propositions of mathematics refer to reality, they are not certain; and as far as they are certain, they do not refer to reality."

(He said this because he realized that even scientists frequently drift into confusion about how representations/attempts at map-making, etc., relate to primary sources of phenomena.)

What goes on in computers—like mathematics—is also hermetic, and thus is not a great basis for internalizing the outlook of science. As with trying to teach music from a book without having the learners sing and play or even hear sounds, this quite misses what things are actually about.

The reality of what’s needed puts a great burden on most families and most public schooling. It involves a lot more work by everyone concerned. This has not happened.

To return to the book as an analogy. Some books will inspire some children (and some parents and some teachers) to start the physical and mental actions that will help them take on the outlooks of the most important human creations: not just science, but music, and other arts; really difficult to handle “softer but critical sciences” (such as anthopology, etc.). “The softer the science the tougher the scientist has to be!”

In long ago talks I used to point out that “The music is not in the piano”. Acting as though it is misses the actual Art form.

Can you come up with a parallel saying for the computer? “The ____ is not in the computer!”

??

Added Jan 11th 2026

Quite a few commenters responded with “parallel sayings” from the above template.

I should explain that I put this in to highlight a difference between a real teacher and a “question answerer” (I am much more of the latter than the former). My friend Neil Postman (RIP) when a grad student used to follow McLuhan around from talk to talk, and noted that Marshall never responded directly to a question or a criticism, but instead said “How about this one?” and would come forth with another paradoxial Zen-Koan-like aphorism. Neil said “I finally realized that McLuhan cared most about whether the audience was thinking at all — and was thus doing what was most important about a great teacher helping students”.

I like to answer questions — as well as I’m able — but almost never take the time and care to try “real teaching” — it’s not clear that it fits into the Quora style and expectations. This experiment was interesting, and thanks to all who responded.

## How was the design process in Xerox Park? How does Alan Kay's process look in his creative work? What does he think about the current design processes?

*https://www.quora.com/How-was-the-design-process-in-Xerox-Park-How-does-Alan-Kays-process-look-in-his-creative-work-What-does-he-think-about-the-current-design-processes/answer/Alan-Kay-11*

First a simple answer to the question, and then to why the question needs to be changed.

Ans: The design process at Parc was basically systems-oriented and derived from best practices, mostly from the ARPA community in the 60s. The most important addition to this was that the Parc researchers agreed amongst themselves to “engineer every invention to be made and usable by at least 100 users. I.e. the Ethernet had to support 100 devices, the personal computer we made had to be manifest as at least 100 machines (actually it grew to about 2000), SW systems had to be supported and documented for at least 100 users (so outside the research group), etc. Another feature common to all the projects at Parc was “never a fatal error”, meaning not losing work regardless of where failures occured (this was done pretty well via many different solutions).

Marshall McLuhan famously said “Don’t ask whether something is Good or Bad, Right or Wrong, True or False—try to Find Out What Is Going On!”.

He meant that judgments are what humans like to make, but they forget that they are always relative to contexts, many of which are invisible to the point of being thought of as “normal reality” rather than arbitrary beliefs.

For example, the consequence of most bugs at Xerox Parc and earlier was not much more than daily annoyances—today the consequences of too many bugs are human deaths (e.g. CrowdStrike’s victims were not just millions of computers for days, but about 2500 hospitals with emergency rooms and IRs, the 737 Max Autopilot, etc.).

The context has changed since the great research decades of the 60s and 70s. In extremis, we could say that the main theme in computing research back then was helping humans think more clearly and strongly, and, today, the main theme for the 21st century could/should well be “human safety”, both with regard to computing, and with the industrial revolution in general.

However, the generally buggy nature of HW and SW back then (and miniscule capacity that tempted “logical brinksmanship” (as Dykstra put it)), along with fairly simple OSs that were understood to be poor, etc., meant that many of the best researchers back then were highly conversant with systems and how they were different from algorithms, and—partially aided by the designing of the ARPAnet, Ethernet, and Internet, the Apollo SW, transmission errors in general, etc.,—were very concerned about dealing detecting and correcting errors, and especially to find ways to allow critical systems to be “eternally up”.

This was still thinking in the small contexts of the time—but the needs were visible and the researchers could see them.

There has been a qualitative shift in scaling, reach, and potential harm since then, to the point where we need to introduce new contexts for thinking about “What’s Going On?”.

A large principle is “Duty Of Care”, which has been in use in Medicine and Engineering for centuries, but which wan’t much of an issue in computing 50–60 years ago (or today!). The central idea is that we should have the right to expect more than “average human abilities and fallibilities” from our physicians and structure and vehicle builders. We don’t want people who can only apply Band-Aids to do open heart surgery. We don’t want people who can only make a dog house to design our apartment buildings and airplanes. Etc.

The awareness of a large context change should change what and how we are judging. For example, we could be saying about today’s so-called “AI”: it doesn’t matter whether it is good or bad, right or wrong, or true or false, what’s important about it is the reach and scaling of how humans react to such a new (to them) and not understandable mass media technology, that has no provisions for “Duty Of Care”, no “Surgeon General’s warnings, and can easily be tied into other non-Duty-Of-Care disasters such as social media.

We could say—similarly about CrowdStrike—what matters is not what it was supposed to do (us “AI” to ward of outside SW attacks), but that it is a wide spread independent set of processes with no sense of human beings, what it is, what it’s intentions need to be, etc. In other words, it is one of many “AI”s that is powerful but completely lacks any sense of what it should and should not be doing—this is a kind of highly dangerous stupidity. Thousands of old style unit tests will not help.

These are a few of many cases of Einstein’s observation that “We cannot solve our problems using the same kinds of thinking that we used to create them!”

I don’t have any impression that many (most?) of today’s companies and their computerists are either (a) even thinking about this, and (b) are up to the task if they were.

## What does Alan Kay think about an Azarrbaijani jazz?

*https://www.quora.com/What-does-Alan-Kay-think-about-an-Azarrbaijani-jazz/answer/Alan-Kay-11*

I had not heard of “Azarrbaijani jazz” until asked this question. So I looked it up in wikipedia:

This was not very informative. However, YouTube (as usual) came through with many examples I listened to — these were from various periods starting in the 1930s through today.

I realize that I don’t know enough to glean whether the YouTube examples were typical or not.

I quite liked much of what I heard. This is because my jazz tastes involve definable harmonic structures with improvisation over the chord patterns. And this is what I heard here. I’m not so fond of “passage work over cluster chords” (which is one of the ways American jazz went after bebop).

To oversimplify, the harmonic structures and substitutions I heard are very recognizable and nice to hear. The melodic structures retained some of the character of traditional Azerbaijani music — in many cases transferred to the piano — this was interesting to hear: the tremelo playing of plectrum instruments to the piano led to very novel lines, and — combined with the rich harmonic structures — I found it very pleasing to listen to.

## Was the work of Adele Goldberg and others, introducing children to programming with Smalltalk, not seen as a duplication of Papert's work at MIT? Why a new teaching language? Why not just teach the children LOGO?

*https://www.quora.com/Was-the-work-of-Adele-Goldberg-and-others-introducing-children-to-programming-with-Smalltalk-not-seen-as-a-duplication-of-Paperts-work-at-MIT-Why-a-new-teaching-language-Why-not-just-teach-the-children-LOGO/answer/Alan-Kay-11*

Short answer to the question because the context turned out to be long.

1. We did duplicate a fair amount of Papert’s and Solomon’s work at MIT — as scientists usually do for (a) learning the details of the work, and (b) to see if we could get the same results (both of these worked out).

2. A series of new teaching languages from both MIT and Parc, because (a) we didn’t know what would work best, especially for the deeper goals both groups had (b) multiple perspectives are generally a good route for both solving, and especially problem finding (c) we shared ideas and arguments because we got more synergies on what we didn’t understand that way (d) this worked well because neither group tended to rivalries.

3. Neither LOGO nor Smalltalk was the answer to what we wanted to accomplish, they proved to be just starting points.

As is so often the case, the actual past history of ideas is more complex and a longer story than fits in a “short answer” forum like Quora.

The Association for Computing Machinery (ACM) has sponsored longer histories. You could look in their History of Programming Languages (HOPL) series for a more detailed sense of how ideas came about, were shared and used, etc. written by the main inventors. For example HOPL I has LISP and JOSS and Simula. The first two were the main precursors of LOGO, and all four came before and were big influences on Smalltalk (whose history is in HOPL II). The HOPL IV book has extended histories of LOGO and a large separate history of Smalltalk implementations.

LOGO itself was first made as a combination of LISP power and JOSS friendliness by Wally Feurzig and Danny Bobrow at BBN to help children learn about human languages. There is a book by them that precedes the “Seymour era”. Seymour Papert was a consultant there and Cynthia Solomon worked there. Seymore had a special inspired way of looking at things, and Cynthia could make things happen, especially with children.

It was seeing this work in 1968 that got me to switch my interests from adults and personal computing to concentrating on children. This was primarily because Seymour’s big idea was that children making things out of “computer stuff” at an early age could positively affect their world view of modern thinking, especially mathematical thinking. I thought this was truly a great insight, and that his and Cynthia’s approach was terrific.

I had a degree in mathematics, and this helped understand the great path they were undertaking. However, I also had a degree in molecular biology, and this brought some of the perspectives of scientific thinking to my own ponderings. One of these was the tradeoffs between math and science as well expressed by Einstein in 1921 in a lecture to physicists in Berlin:

" ... as far as the propositions of mathematics refer to reality, they are not certain; and as far as they are certain, they do not refer to reality."

My take on this is that learning “pure reasoning” is quite dangerous for humans without understanding that it is hermetic and needs to be grounded in science (which is “hermetic with warnings attached”).

Smalltalk came from notions about the usefulness of “multiple similar parametized entities” that would allow many ideas to be thought about as instantiations of whole dynamic ideas. My first thought after seeing what Seymour and Cynthia were doing was the idea of a children’s tablet computer with the children being able to program a game they would like to play — like SpaceWar — that would require them to investigate and model some of how the real world seemed to work — and that both spaceships and “torpedoes” could be modeled as a single idea if you could instantiate ideas.

Instantiation of objects appeared very early in Sketchpad (‘62), and then Simula (‘65). Of dynamic processes in the early 60s multiprogramming and time-sharing OSs. My early idea (‘66) was that this could be used as a universal way to describe and build arbitrary processes in a clean fashion. I used it in my PhD thesis (‘69) and then started to see if there was a children’s language that could be made. The first one I did was called “SLOGO” for “Simulation LOGO”.

This was a very fun time in computing — both in general and especially for computerists who could see that it could be specially for children and education. There were no rivalries, everyone had different points of view, and freely shared their favorite approaches.

Everyone realized — more or less — that (a) different children needed different approaches (b) Montessori was a pretty good starting place in general (c) Piaget’s and Bruner’s approaches to children’s thinking was also a rich perspective (d) No one knew enough (e) lots of actual work with children would be required, etc.

For example, “we knew that we didn’t know” what kind of programming system would help children be more than programmers (it had already been noted that “programmers” didn’t automatically acquire much if any special perspectives and outlooks beyond simple “instrumental” outlooks (that were even very often counterproductive).

I was very lucky to find and attract Adele away from Stanford to be a co-manager in my group at Parc. She was a complete powerhouse in all directions, had superpowers, could do everything, etc. (she later won the ACM Software Systems Award, and still later became the second woman president of the ACM, is now in the prestigious Computer Museum Hall of Fellows, etc.).

We did duplicate a lot of what Seymour and Cynthia did — both to learn, and to have enough context for additional thoughts. Adele thought of a great way to teach objects directly (and first) that was very fruitful, and led to the children being able not just to program, but to make tool frameworks (this was partly because, once you understand instantiation, many things that are difficult to handle in a data-procedural language, become quite easy).

In fact, neither LOGO nor Smalltalk were good enough for the original visions. Both groups continued to make new designs. The head systems “machers” were Brian Silverman for LOGO and Dan Ingalls for Smalltalk. (Dan won the Grace Hopper Award for inventing BitBlt, the ACM Software Systems Award for Smalltalk, and is now in the prestigious Computer Museum Hall of Fellows, etc.)

Later, important pedagogical work involving Smalltalk was done by Brian Harvey (his three books “Computer Science Logo Style” are three of my favorites).

Mitchel Reznick did an important thesis that involved “massively parallel” entities that were instantiations (StarLOGO). Hypercard by Bill Atkinson and Dan Winkler had many important insights. We did many systems also.

The basic thrust here is that “when you don’t know how to do something, do many things!”

At Disney we tried a new angle, which resulted in the Etoys system (programmed in Smalltalk). This used a very uniform approach to instantiable entities and an easy approach to parallel models. This turned out to be extremely simple and powerful at the same time.

This was the first one that I felt was workable for the kids — 25 years after the start of the project! — and could really embody the mathematical/practical outlook of science. Mitchel Reznick wanted to do a followon, and we got NSF to fund it. The result was Scratch (and it was first programmed in Smalltalk).

One can learn a lot from observing what happened with Scratch. (a) it was very successful, and it’s possible to say why (b) it is a very large example that there has to be a well thought out curriculum to go along with a new tool, or the results will be mostly mundane (which they were).

## Is it possible to design a self-consistent computational universe where a small Forth-like meta-model provides the semantic substrate, similar to how Smalltalk provided an object substrate?

*https://www.quora.com/Is-it-possible-to-design-a-self-consistent-computational-universe-where-a-small-Forth-like-meta-model-provides-the-semantic-substrate-similar-to-how-Smalltalk-provided-an-object-substrate/answer/Alan-Kay-11*

Sure. You could start your thinking and learning by looking at how LISPs have been implemented.

There are lots of possible meanings for “meta” here, including: reflection, the kernel in itself, etc.

It’s worth pondering that a really useful kernel needs to start off with “What is actually needed” perspectives regarding allocation of storage & levels, processor, safety, security, etc. (Most computer folks go directly at programs and computation, but — paradoxically — the “goodness down the road” will depend as much on these properties as it does on what most people think of as “computation”. You basically have to redefine “computation” and implement it as part of your virtual machine to have a decent chance with the scalings we now have to deal with.

I would try to read and understand the first 100 pages or so of “The Art of the Metaobject Protocol” book for useful perspectives. Another “first 100 pages gem” is the first 105 pages of David Fisher’s 1970 CMU thesis: “A control definition language”.

FORTH already has a fairly simple/easy bootstrap from scratch on a new machine. Another “meta thought” would be how to avoid having the kernel definitions be in machine code (and specific to the machine) and, instead, find a machine independent way to define the kernel — presumably you’d like to have it be FORTH — but to have enough extra mechanism in your architecture to allow you to write a meta-translator that would make the resulting system machine-independent.

Smalltalk first used kernels implemented in machine code, but then was able to write the kernel in itself, and then a compiler into lower level forms — this isolated the non-Smalltalk part to a very small part of the system.

Some of the experts who have done great work along these lines are: Dan Ingalls, John Maloney, Ian Piumarta, etc.

(This latter process can be a lot of fun to try to figure out elegant and simple ways to deal with the fact that — at some point — you will have to grapple with something that isn’t FORTH in order to get it running on a given computer (the idea is to keep this both minimum and as simple as possible).)

## All of the greats and experts in CS and programming say that A. Kay's Smalltalk is the best PL and PE ever. If it's a clear winner, then why is it not used widely in the science and industry?

*https://www.quora.com/All-of-the-greats-and-experts-in-CS-and-programming-say-that-A-Kays-Smalltalk-is-the-best-PL-and-PE-ever-If-its-a-clear-winner-then-why-is-it-not-used-widely-in-the-science-and-industry/answer/Alan-Kay-11*

In “The Early History of Smalltalk” written for SIGPLAN as a ramp up to HOPL II, I made it clear that the Smalltalk that was released — and is the one people mean today when they say “Smalltalk” — was much more due to Dan Ingalls — for much of its design and implementation — and to Adele Goldberg — as a co-manager of our research group — for getting it out in a form that could spread and be understood. I started the project and wrote the first “math for a Smalltalk” that showed how to do a minimal bootstrap, and contributed a few more things.

Dan, Adele, and I were jointly awarded the ACM Software Systems Award for this.

Smalltalk was originally invented in the 70s to be used in the 80s with HW architectures that we thought would follow the Burroughs architectures into VLSI CPUs. (These allow very high level languages to be small and efficient.)

This didn’t happen, and C would up being a much lower level language approach to dealing with what Intel, etc., did provide. VHLLs like Smalltalk and LISP suffered …

## If Alan Kay were to modify his Squeakland.org reading list, what would he add or remove? http://www.squeakland.org/resources/books/readingList.jsp

*https://www.quora.com/If-Alan-Kay-were-to-modify-his-Squeakland-org-reading-list-what-would-he-add-or-remove-http-www-squeakland-org-resources-books-readingList-jsp/answer/Alan-Kay-11*

I was originally — in the 80s — asked by a company for my top 10 books. I responded by saying most heavy readers like me don’t have a top 10, and then made the mistake of providing about 500 titles that I thought were worth reading. This list has passed through many hands since I last touched it. Now we are about 40 years later, and of course I’ve kept on reading …

However — on reflection — I realized I should have replied with something more general than a list — that the list I provided was much too much about my own educational catalyzers, rather than how to help others find their own pathways … .

I think the best use of books is to give us a wider range of ideas to possibly follow up than we might have by ourselves. Because any written down sentences can be prefixed by either or both of two phrases — (a) “It is definitely true that …” and/or (b) “It is definitely not true that … “ — we can readily see that books can be about lots of ideas and assert many different sides of any question …

This means that books — writing — is very dangerous without also setting up ways to deal with the ideas, especially ones about the universe we seem to be living in. Modern science provides some very useful tools for not getting confused (as Einstein pointed out to a group of scientists in 1921 when he said " ... as far as the propositions of mathematics refer to reality, they are not certain; and as far as they are certain, they do not refer to reality." Geometry and Experience, Lecture before the Prussian Academy of Sciences, January 27, 1921.)

But it’s clear that we also need something similar to deal with ethics and morals — and this is much more difficult because it is tantamount to needing to create (design) the ethical equivalent of the physical universe which is already here. This “psychical universe” has to be generally agreed on in order to work (the nice thing about the physical universe is that it can be investigated from scratch).

In any case, what is needed to deal with ideas — and especially in the context of humanity — is something that works much better than blind belief in whatever ideas are appealing. All of us are humans in a single species, and we all need this. However, we are all interestingly different: to the extent that we need to find our own intellectual journeys to build “better than mere believing minds”.

When I was a kid, I used to roam the stacks in our public library — and my grandfather’s book shelves — to read books “on general principles”. As I mentioned in another Quora answer, many of the books I thought were not very good, actually contributed to the whole experience (in part because they provided a view of the larger human experience, and that parts of it seemed to be really misguided — and this meant that the parts I liked could be misguided also!

And all of this helped with what reading brought to my own growth experiences …

Because — as humans — we suffer from many cognitive biases — and a deep one is “confirmation bias” — it’s critical — no matter how much we think something is true — to maintain a little area where doubt can operate. This little patch in our minds is the soil in which progress in thinking can be grown.

This is what I wished I had told those who originally asked me for “my list” …

## What were the advantages and disadvantages of having complete control over hardware and software designs at Parc in the pursuit of developing personal computing?

*https://www.quora.com/What-were-the-advantages-and-disadvantages-of-having-complete-control-over-hardware-and-software-designs-at-Parc-in-the-pursuit-of-developing-personal-computing/answer/Alan-Kay-11*

Larry Stewart’s answer to a related question covered some of the useful details (he was also at Parc and a central part of many projects there).

First, we didn’t have “complete control” over the HW — for example, during the most productive decade of Parc we almost exclusively used chips made by others (most would be called “medium scale ICs”), and the only VLSIs we used were for memories. So e.g. most CPUs etc., were board sized or several boards of MSIs. Virtually all of the HW critical architectures were completely designed and built at Parc.

There were various ways to look at this. My slogan was “Hardware is just Software crystallized early”, and was thus an intrinsic part of the software design process.

The stated aim of much of the HW at Parc was to act as “time machines” via using money to make machines today which Moore’s Law would allow to be made many orders of magnitude cheaper in the future. The idea was to develop the SW of the future *now* by being able to run it on “supercomputer” versions today of commodity computers tomorrow.

This made a lot of sense along many dimensions. And that particular time period had just introduced the critical memory HW (MOS DRAMs) which just happened to run from 5–10 times more slowly than the much faster MSI chips. This meant that a microcoded CPU and small superfast memory could be much faster than the general RAM, and that meant that the machine would be able to emulate in microcode many functions that formerly required HW — and further — that if the microcode memory was dynamically loadable (at Parc it was) — then one could emulate many different enivironments and functions at will.

For example, each of the UHL languages done at Parc had its own microcode, bitBlt (the screen painter) had its own microcode, so did the various music/sound processing, etc.

These skills were critical in making HW such as the Ethernet, the laser printer, and their interfaces, etc.

The advantages of all this should be obvious. Even though Moore’s Law would eventually catch up, this approach provided a many years head-start and extreme flexibility by allowing future SW to be thought about as a whole system. Since we were aiming at new kinds of SW, we needed the time and flexibility (and also not to optimize and work around old HW) etc.

The disadvantage was that we had to design and make all the tools, building, testing, etc. In practice, the Parc researchers were more than up to this (quite amazingly so in my opinion), and a number of the most important systems were done in terms of months.

## Who is called the father of modern computers?

*https://www.quora.comhttps://mdwahedjitustechnology.quora.com/Who-is-called-the-father-of-modern-computers-3*

Please tell me in a comment what time frame you mean by “modern” and what you mean by “called the father” (the way it is phrased here implies something like a social vote rather than an appeal to history.

For now, I’ll take “modern” to mean “20th century”, and “called” to mean “is”.

My personal pick would overwhelmingly be Turing. Besides all the interesting theoretical and mathematical ground he covered in his 1936 "On Computable Numbers” paper, it was his “rather engineering” approach that wound up having the greater impact.

As von Neumann later pointed out, it was the universality of interpreting symbols (and symbols of interpretation) placed in the context of simple machinery that suggested a practical route to actually making a universal computer. (What we today call a “von Neumann computer architecture” is actually an almost direct adaptation of the approach Turing used in his paper.)

Both for engineering and philosophy, it turned to be very important that the design suggested “almost no machinery” coupled with lots of “simple marking memory” — this greatly helped both practical building of physical computers *and* ways to thing very large thoughts about layers of abstration.

## In the early days of personal computing, what one platform - if successfully commercialized - could have set computing on a better trajectory than the 1980s micros did? - Details in comments.

*https://www.quora.com/In-the-early-days-of-personal-computing-what-one-platform-if-successfully-commercialized-could-have-set-computing-on-a-better-trajectory-than-the-1980s-micros-did-Details-in-comments/answer/Alan-Kay-11*

I have an urge to provide a decent answer here, but I don’t think I know how to.

This is primarily because (a) of the ways that systems within Moore’s Law can or cannot be developed, and (b) because I think you mean “personal computing” when you say “computing” (and now we are expanding an idea into an even less savvy market than the mainstream market for various sized computers that existed before the 80s).

At Xerox Parc — and even a bit before in the ARPA community — because of the way we thought, did prototyping, etc., we could write down basic numbers for how many bits of what kinds and how many cycles of what kinds would be needed for our conceptions of personal computing to be possible (e.g. it’s important to understand that ARPA-IPTO made personal computing systems on mainframes of various sizes — some of them really large and expensive (“personal computing” is a collection of experiences, etc.)).

The advent of the Intel 1103 DRAMs changed the costs for one very important part of the kinds of experiences we were thinking about. The Alto was a gamble that we could do enough to make real progress in practical personal computing even if some of the other system needs did not come through in time. This barely worked out, but the fact that it did was significant.

It’s worth looking at markets at various times and noting what they were willing and able to pay. An important early market in the mid-70s was for stand-alone dedicated word processing machines. A much more general “Alto III” could be made and sold for a profit at the same price point as a dedicated word processor ca 1976–7. That would have been revolutionary for a while — and would certainly change the perception and perspectives of the market. This would be “personal computing in business” (not “personal computing in consumer-land”).

In the world of consumers, people were willing to pay a fair amount for a house (usually by borrowing), and still a fair amount for an autombile (also usually via a loan). Most products called “consumer products” were much cheaper. Note that the automobile metaphor is worth looking at more closely. If you understood what a computer was and what it could do then you might be able to see it as your personal information vehicle, and be willing to pay the average price of a car ca 1980–2 for one (this was about $9.5K).

There was at least one high quality system of that price happening around that time: the Apple Lisa. My opinion of it was high, and I was happy to use them after I went to Apple. However, the large market wouldn’t accept it, and was willing to do much less for paying much less via the IBM PC. This became a huge barrier for the rest of the decade and beyond.

There were a few late 70s early 80s machines we’d call “workstations” today (and because consumers didn’t want to pay what the Lisa was worth, we have to include the Lisa as a kind of low cost workstation). Besides the “Dande…” workstations made by Parc, there were also several really impressive machines made by 3 Rivers Corp (initally designed by Brian Rosen who had spent time at Parc). There was the “3M” initiative by CMU (1 Million Pixel, 1 MIP, 1 Megabyte RAM) — this is kind of what was needed, but did not fit into what the larger markets were willing to pay.

An interesting “better than Mac” that could have been put in the Mac space was the Amiga …

Moore’s Law predicted that really good personal computers would eventually reach price points that the mass markets would accept. A good idea would have been to wait a few years — but one way to characterize “consumer businesses” is “what can you sell in mass to unsophisticated markets for reasons other than ‘quality’?”

The big problem with this is that bad defacto standards are going to happen — and much much worse — many of these will stick (and some for no good reason at all).

This was especially the case in the 10 years between the early 80s and early 90s. Moore’s Law did go more or less as predicted (and in some important cases — like file storage — vastly exceeded expectations). But many important things needed in operating and development environments and assets and UIs for users, etc., stayed mired in their early weak conceptions of the early 80s. The Web browser was done especially badly (and the Web itself was much too weak an idea).

Basically, no matter what most people thought was going on in the 80s, that decade was really the decade of “locking into not-so-good” and then pretty much staying “not-so-good” (which means “ever worse”) until the present.

A really interesting question — I think — is whether the general unsophistication of most markets (and even most computerists) could ever have been dealt with in a much more positive manner. What we actually got was “a will of the people”. This is what happened with Covid recentily, and with the climate over the 60+ years that experts have known the depth of the problem.

It just hasn’t mattered that — for many important things — experts often do have better ideas about issues, directions and methods. The bizbiz coupled with unsophisticated markets is and has been driving.

## How did early software developers manage to create efficient programs with such limited computing resources?

*https://www.quora.com/How-did-early-software-developers-manage-to-create-efficient-programs-with-such-limited-computing-resources/answer/Alan-Kay-11*

Basically: “every which way” they could think of — and this was actually “highly motivated” by the limitations of computing resources.

For example, I have often shown movies of the amazing 1968 Engelbart “Mother of all demos” with its subsecond response times, pointed out that it was done on a half MIP, 24bit, 192KB time-shared computer with multiple users, and asked “how was this possible?”. Only once in years of asking this question have I ever gotten an accurate answer (interestingly from a student in an audience of undergrads): “Because they *wanted* subsecond response?”

Yep. That was one of their principal goals, and they kept it, no matter what.

Another way to look at this is that the instruction times of even really slow computers, even running interpreters (and losing another factor of 10 or so), are much faster than human nervous systems, so even for interactive systems in the early days — such as “George” on Whirlwind in 1954 — one could get quite good real-time response (if one really wanted it).

And — in general, whether real-time or batch — many of the earliest programmers were also mathematicians, and so had a feeling for both “abstraction” and “deeper meta”.

Also — a bit of apples and oranges here — the most stringent limitation most of the time was “amount of available RAM”. This tended to dominate how programming needed to be done (basically, if you have to swap/overlay from secondary storage, you have killed your average cycle time). One of the most amazing examples of this was done by Hal Laning (the original creator of “George”) for the extremely slow and limited Apollo Guidance Computer for the moon shot project. The basic computer had a memory cycle time of ~16 bits in 12 microseconds with a RAM of 4KB, however many operations were actually done by an interpreter whose pseudocode ran about 50IPS (!)

Another interesting case from the old days is when Engelbart’s group moved to a faster PDP-10 timesharing system, and discovered that making an interpretive “byte-coded” interpretive version of their implementation language (much slower in simple benchmarks), actually ran much faster than optimized compiled code in practice because the tinier p-codes could fit much more easily into the slicing and dicing of memory scheme that the Tenex OS used — thus vastly reducing the need to swap — and thus vastly improving the “system dynamic” and “user experience/perception”.

One of my favorite “bang for the buck” systems from ca 60 years ago was the Meta II compiler-compiler done on an 8K 6-bit byte IBM 1401 computer by Val Schorre at UCLA. This worked because he had really thought through the problem space and had come up with a tiny meta-characterization that had enough range to deal with a wide range of higher level languages (this is basically the “Math Wins!” idea). He was also able to apply the meta-idea to itself to get the pseudo-code for the system that a simple interpreter on the 1401 could run.

He wrote a classic small paper that was able to give explicit implementable examples of the meta system, a teaching example, and two sample “Algol-level” languages. The system in itself is fun to contemplate:

This is the link to the entire paper

Basic idea here is that there is often — even “usually” — some “meta math” under most problems. Spending some time trying to articulate and represent this will often result in much tinier, easier to understand and debug systems.

## Computer scientist Edsger W. Dijkstra said that “It is far more likely that the programming occupation will become extinct than that programmers will ever approach professional status.” What did Dijkstra mean by that and do you agree with Dijkstra?

*https://www.quora.com/Computer-scientist-Edsger-W-Dijkstra-said-that-It-is-far-more-likely-that-the-programming-occupation-will-become-extinct-than-that-programmers-will-ever-approach-professional-status-What-did-Dijkstra-mean-by-that/answer/Alan-Kay-11*

I’ll start by saying that I don’t clearly understand the English as simply stated.

However, three things might help us (a) English was not Edsger’s native language (b) he was very proud of his skills in English (c) he delighted in coming up with snide remarks (one of his good friends was Bob Barton, who also liked to do this).

I read this as “programmers will never approach professional status” — and — “the programming occupation will never become extinct (too bad)”!

He desired the process of getting computers to “do what we mean!” to be rather like the mathematics he was used to when getting his PhD in mathematical physics. In his own words:

After having programmed for some three years, I had a discussion with A. van Wijngaarden, who was then my boss at the Mathematical Center in Amsterdam, a discussion for which I shall remain grateful to him as long as I live. The point was that I was supposed to study theoretical physics at the University of Leiden simultaneously, and as I found the two activities harder and harder to combine, I had to make up my mind, either to stop programming and become a real, respectable theoretical physicist, or to carry my study of physics to a formal completion only, with a minimum of effort, and to become....., yes what? A programmer? But was that a respectable profession? For after all, what was programming? Where was the sound body of knowledge that could support it as an intellectually respectable discipline? I remember quite vividly how I envied my hardware colleagues, who, when asked about their professional competence, could at least point out that they knew everything about vacuum tubes, amplifiers and the rest, whereas I felt that, when faced with that question, I would stand empty-handed.

He had “bitten the apple” and gotten hooked. And the dual attractions and repulsions of math on the one side and programming on the other stayed with him his whole life.

It was his pristineness towards the former that got him to disparage the latter — even though that was the path he also had taken …

*https://www.quora.com/Was-one-byte-ever-less-than-eight-bits-in-the-past/answer/Alan-Kay-11*

When I started “programming as a job” in the US Air Force (ca 1962), the most general meaning for a “byte” was “a contiguous field of bits in a word that was smaller in size than the word”.

I still remember feeling annoyed when IBM redefined the term to mean an 8-bit entity (I remember this from 1964 when System 360 was announced — however, IBM could have forced the redefinition before this).

The Wikipedia article is rather wishy-washy about this. I think that my definition in the first paragraph is actually correct.

## Is programming learned inductively or deductively?

*https://www.quora.com/Is-programming-learned-inductively-or-deductively-1/answer/Alan-Kay-11*

I don’t feel I completely understand this question (or, perhaps, don’t understand the intention behind the question).

But we can certainly start by comparing various kinds of reasoning already addressed in Quora:

Let me add an additional one or two: “projective reasoning” — this is similar to “abductive reasoning”. It is familiar in both mathematics and programming as a kind of “feeling” about a situation (in programming it often occurs as a “sense of difficulty or ease” when a problem is mentioned). It is also likely related to what is called “forward reasoning”: to take definitions/premises and drive them “forward” using logical operations to reach conclusions (so: similar to deduction, but driving “outwards”).

My first paying job as a programmer/coder was in 1962 — so 63 years ago as of this writing — as an enlisted man in the US Air Force. They had a test to screen for possible aptitudes. Those who passed were trained by IBM in a single dense wall to wall week, and then sent back to base to write and debug code (i.e. the rest of the training was “on the job training”).

From my own personal experience, I would say the answer to this question is “All of the above (including my additions), and more”. One example of “more” is that it was common enough back then for the hardware to have glitches — sometimes “intermittant glitches” — so that one could not completly rely that executions were completely deterministic.

I think I might instead say that “Learning programming is both learning how to “solve problems”, and especially how to “find problems”, mixed in with much more “design” than one appreciates at first”.

## What are your thoughts on a future where code is represented as a structured model, rather than text? Do you think that AI-powered coding assistants benefit from that?

*https://www.quora.com/What-are-your-thoughts-on-a-future-where-code-is-represented-as-a-structured-model-rather-than-text-Do-you-think-that-AI-powered-coding-assistants-benefit-from-that/answer/Alan-Kay-11*

First, it’s worth noting that the “syntax recognition” phase of most compilers already does build a “structured model”, often in what used to be called a “canonical form” (an example of this might be a “pseudo-function tree” where every elementary process description is put into the same form — so both “a + b” and “for i := 1 to x do […]” are rendered as

plus(a, b)      for(i, 1, x, […])

in structures, such as:

   +                     for

  / \    and            ⁄ / | \ 

 a   b                i 1  x  []

i.e. “operator like things” at the nodes …

Another canonical form could be Lisp S-expressions, etc.

These structures are made precisely to allow programs to “reason” about some parts of lower level meaning, and in many cases to rearrange the structure to preserve meaning but to make the eventual code that is generated more efficient.

Long ago in the 50s this was even thought of as a kind of “AI” and this association persisted into the 60s. Several Turing Awards were given for progress on this kind of “machine reasoning”.

Most coding assistants — with or without “modern “AI” — also do reasoning and manipulation of structures.

It’s important to realize that “modern “AI” doesn’t understand human level meanings any better today (in many cases: worse!). So it is not going to be able to serve as much of a helper in a general coding assistant.

A slogan that might help you get past the current fads is:

NOT DATA … BUT MEANING!
