## Why did Japan’s Fifth Generation Computer Systems project fail commercially? Are any of its concepts and advances presently being utilized?

*https://www.quora.com/Why-did-Japan-s-Fifth-Generation-Computer-Systems-project-fail-commercially-Are-any-of-its-concepts-and-advances-presently-being-utilized/answer/Alan-Kay-11*

The answer by Marcus Triska sums up much of the history and context rather well

I will just add to this a few impressions from the early years of this project. The Japanese project leaders were quite open about the project and invited Ed Feigenbaum to select 20 or 30 American computer scientists to visit periodically and discuss the project, etc. This group included Ed, John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky, many other luminaries in the field, and a “fringe member” (myself).

These visits were quite fun, and the American group itself got along quite well (we all liked to argue in a fairly reasonable way).

The Japanese scientists in the 80s adopted the sensible approach of ARPA/Parc in the 60s and 70s of trying to define and write enough SW to be able to design HW that would optimize difficult important parts that were not served by conventional architectures. The large scale and ability of the Japanese government to both fund and “coax” companies to cooperate at various levels and standards started off well.

Some of the details were doubtful (IMO, etc.). Some of us felt that it would be a better idea to invent a new language that would be more suitable than PROLOG as a base for the large goals (there were a number of ideas in PROLOG that were quite good, and some that needed to be reinvented better). One of the eventual fallouts was Shapiro’s “Concurrent Prolog”, which was a much cleaner, better, way to approach this genre of ideas.

I meant to add this in the original answer: Every computerist should know about and have read with a “research eye” Kazunori Ueda’s excellent paper: “Logic/Constraint Programming and Concurrency: The hard-won lessons of the Fifth Generation Computer project”. Many of the issues and suggestions here are very worth pondering in the light of today’s problems (i.e. you will get a lot from reading this regardless of whether you agree or not).

A perhaps too simple bottom line is that quite a bit of good research got done — but there was also a lot of constriction to move quickly to showing practicality. It might be possible to do this at the pace that was attempted, but I’ve never witnessed it. The real learning curves in my own experience actually — unfortunately — take much longer than the pace of business.

I think this project — overall — helped computer science in general and Japanese computer science in particular. To me it was a research project, and did turn up considerable knowledge of various useful kinds.

I don’t know the answer to this (I’ve always tried to work with colleagues who are more able than I am — going back to playing in bands, theatre, tennis, science, etc.). Also, ARPA-IPTO had the interesting idea of creating groups of smart people where no-one was the smartest in the room (I think most of us still thought it was Butler Lampson).

I don’t know how one would go about determining “below average” … a much better idea and question could be about “less able”, where the goal would be to help the growth of “more able”. This is definitely a better way to think about children, and I think it works for adults also (in other words, keep the potential of others in mind and alive).

A key notion of “team” is that every member winds up able to get over the bar (because every member is helping every member get over the bar).

A big shift I made in my 20s was from changing my self rating as to how I was doing based on “results” to assessing “quality of effort”. This worked much better because I was much more in control of “quality of effort”, and not worrying about “results” plus higher “quality of effort” tended to produce higher quality results (but now I didn’t care so much about the latter, etc.)

## Since von Neumann invented the merge sort algo in 1945, just before ENIAC was introduced in 1946, what does Alan Kay think motivated him to explore sorting algos when computers were still so new and HLL didn't yet exist?

*https://www.quora.com/Since-von-Neumann-invented-the-merge-sort-algo-in-1945-just-before-ENIAC-was-introduced-in-1946-what-does-Alan-Kay-think-motivated-him-to-explore-sorting-algos-when-computers-were-still-so-new-and-HLL-didnt-yet/answer/Alan-Kay-11*

Richard Norman has already provided a nice short accurate answer to this question.

The notion of “algorithm” goes back at least to the early Greeks (and several are given by Euclid).

Another area that extensively used algorithms before programmable digital computers was “Relaxation Methods in Engineering and Science” — the classic Southwell books date back to the 1940s.

Many of the early processes that ENIAC ran were ballistic calculations that had been done for years by humans using desktop numerical calculators.

HLLs are not needed for programming or for carrying out algorithms. However, a kind of HLL (Flowcharting) was used in many areas to provide an HL portrayal of various calculation schemes.

## What does Alan Kay suggest here: "Computing is not about clocks, it's about biology". How come the essence of computing is more about the way living organisms evolve?

*https://www.quora.com/What-does-Alan-Kay-suggest-here-Computing-is-not-about-clocks-its-about-biology-How-come-the-essence-of-computing-is-more-about-the-way-living-organisms-evolve/answer/Alan-Kay-11*

I wouldn’t have said the “quoted phrase” in the way it is stated (so the quotes likely mean something else). And I wouldn’t have said “The essence of computing is more about the way living things evolve” (I would have used a term like “work”, instead of “evolve”).

In many talks, long ago, I have shown a picture with the title “From Gears To Biology” as a metaphor for a qualitative shift in thinking about computer systems — from early-bound, tightly coupled rather small mechanisms — like clocks — to late-bound, loosely coupled rather large mechanisms — like living organisms. In computing, this happened within a single lifetime, and many parts of computing are still stuck in the earlier metaphor.

We can see the difficulties that general computing has had in adjusting to the great scalings brought by Moore’s Law. For example, the “going off the Internet of Facebook/Meta” and the recent “Crowdstrike” (what a strange title for a computer system!) debacle.

Pondering the qualitative differences between gear-like systems and biology-like systems can be very helpful in thinking more clearly about dealing with great scalings in computing systems.

## What does Alan Kay think about ADHD in adults? Should it be controlled with medication?

*https://www.quora.com/What-does-Alan-Kay-think-about-ADHD-in-adults-Should-it-be-controlled-with-medication/answer/Alan-Kay-11*

I don’t have the medical background to answer generally.

However, I have many creative close friends who have ADHD. Most of them use the drugs to help (they do help greatly) to cope with many actions in the world that are difficult for those with ADHD.

When they are deeply within creative phases of their life that work well off the drugs, but not well with them (for example, acting in theatre), they often go off the drugs. I have a very close friend who uses the drug in the morning, and lets it wear off for theatre rehearsals in the evening.

These are just annecdotes, and certainly don’t cover the general case.

However, all of my ADHD friends look at the drugs as a godsend, and all whom I know use the drugs wisely.

## What is Alan Kay’s view on analytic idealism by Bernardo Kastrup?

*https://www.quora.com/What-is-Alan-Kay-s-view-on-analytic-idealism-by-Bernardo-Kastrup/answer/Alan-Kay-11*

I’m sure that I need to read his forthcoming book in order to attempt an answer:

Analytic Idealism in a Nutshell: A Straightforward Summary of the 21st Century's Only Plausible Metaphysics

I’ve ordered it — it is not out yet — due to arrive Nov 1st this year (2024).

However, I should reveal a personal prejudice against what I understand is the basic idea. As with most prejudices, it doesn’t have much substantive behind it, but I’ll be trying to keep this in mind when I read the book.

See you in November …

Here are my reactions as of Nov 6th.

I got his book — Analytic Idealism in a Nutshell: A Straightforward Summary of the 21st Century's Only Plausible Metaphysics — and have read it.

The ideas in it are put forth as an essay into Philosophy, particularly focused on Metaphysics (the nature of Being itself).

Wikipedia’s definition is good enough:

Metaphysics is the study of the most general features of reality, including existence, objects and their properties, possibility and necessity, space and time, change, causation, and the relation between matter and mind. It is one of the oldest branches of philosophy.

I wonder if I understand enough about the general subject area — Philosophy in general, and Metaphysics in particular — to make it worthwhile to share my opinions? My thought patterns are primarily within the general outlooks of science, math, engineering, and some of the arts: musical, visual, theatric, literate, etc.

I like — and subscribe to — Einstein’s reminder to scientists in his 1921 talk in Berlin:

" ... as far as the propositions of mathematics refer to reality, they are not certain; and as far as they are certain, they do not refer to reality."

Geometry and Experience, Lecture before the Prussian Academy of Sciences, January 27, 1921

Kastrup starts out with his version of this idea — one I’ve also used many times in talks — that

what we think of as “out there” is actually going on in our brains: “in here”, between our ears.

We create a kind of a map that is its own internal world, and — if we are sophisticated — we realize that our map should not be called “reality”, and at best we have to negotiate between the limitations of our mappings and the phenomenal evidence we can detect. This internal world each human has is sometimes called our “Private Universe”.

Kastrup likens the internal map to a dashboard inside a hermetically sealed airplane where the instruments provide enough information to fly the plane, but do not at all resemble what we’d see if we could look outside the plane (this is a quite good example/analogy).

Kastrup adds several other postulates in his Introduction. Here are his additional four (partially quoting):

There is an external world out there, beyond our physical minds

This world unfolds on its own, according to its own inherent dispositions, and reveals some phenomena our senses (and sense aids) can pick up

Human reason can recognize and model what it thinks are regularities in this phenomena, and in some cases can predict future phenomena

Complex phenomena can be “sufficiently accounted for in terms of simpler ones” (basically non-linear reductionism).

I think most scientists — including me — would agree that these five are highly likely. Kastrup calls these realism.

The writing style of this book is nicely clear, but very repetitious. There is an air of “I need to explain this many times because you are probably not understanding”. The last part might very well be the case, but repetition doesn’t help.

And, he starts arguing right away. It is not at all clear to me that his arguments (a) work, and/or (b) perhaps can be made at all. I am prejudiced in favor of essays which spend a lot of their front matter in exposition and follow this groundwork by argument. This is not done here.

I will try to fit the rest of this within a Quora-sized (albeit one still too long) answer.

One way to approach this is to ask whether his initial premises — which I agree with — actually allow his thesis — that Being is a kind of universal mentality that is very unlike the internal mappings that physical scientists try to make of Nature — to be successfully argued.

In Philosophical terms, the 5 premises above are essentially epistemological. Wikipedia again:

Epistemology, the philosophical study of the nature, origin, and limits of human knowledge

Taken together, it looks as though these premises of Analytic Idealism make it difficult to do more than claim any ultimate knowledge about anything “out there”. I.e. I think that Kastrup can claim his thesis as a proposition — but, given the premises, I don’t think he can substantiate his claim. As Einstein pointed out, logic/math/language/inference with the aim of “certainly” with regard to chains of thought will not refer to “reality” but only — if done as well as possible — to the consistency of the arguments.

For example, an argument of the form “because the thing in question is not this, this or this, it must be *that*” only works in reasoning/logic/math, etc., if you can first show that you have enumerated all the candidates and eliminated all but one.

The needed enumeration is not done here, and I don’t think it can be done.

A book that I’ve enjoyed very much — and which provoked much mulling — was Julian Jaynes’ “The Origin Of Consciousness In The Breakdown Of The Bicameral Mind” (TOOCITBOTBM). It is perhaps my favorite of this kind of book. I doubt its conclusions, but thinking about the issues, evidence, and forms of argument have. quite widened my thoughts over the years.

Analytic Idealism In A Nutshell is also a book that provokes mulling. The subject matter is a few levels more murky and abstract than TOOCITBOTBM, but trying to understand what is being attempted and pondering whether its arguments actually hold water can be quite enjoyable, and to some extent, illuminating.

## How does Alan Kay view Don Norman's perspective on humanity-centered design?

*https://www.quora.com/How-does-Alan-Kay-view-Don-Normans-perspective-on-humanity-centered-design/answer/Alan-Kay-11*

I’ve known Don Norman as a colleague and friend for more than 50 years, and I value all his perspectives whether I agree (most of the time I do) or not (sometimes I don’t).

Don has had a long illustrious career centered in Cognitive Psychology and associated “human factors”.

Don was a consultant for “The Learning Research Group” that I set up at Parc, and contributed greatly to many parts of our research thinking. He liked to argue (in good ways), and so did we, and this wound up covering lots of ground. He and I also worked together at Apple in the 80s. We have remained friends.

Etc.

A bottom line is that Don’s ideas are a must for anyone thinking about systems which involve people, and especially for systems where attempts are made to better fit them to human users and uses.

I’m being a bit elliptical here because the area of “actual UI design” — though there are a few priniciples — is still done best by many experiments with many design variations. This means that a new UI designer needs to absorb an enormous amount of lore — especially from great designers — *and* has to be willing to do the new large amount of work to bring a new UI to useful life.

Don’s perspectives are thus deeply important to learn and understand.

## Why didn't Doug Engelbart's chording keyset become a standard interface like the mouse did? It requires more training, but would have a dramatic impact on user performance.

*https://www.quora.com/Why-didnt-Doug-Engelbarts-chording-keyset-become-a-standard-interface-like-the-mouse-did-It-requires-more-training-but-would-have-a-dramatic-impact-on-user-performance/answer/Alan-Kay-11*

Here’s the classic Engelbart NLS interface:

This was the result of testing many alternative designs. A basic principle was that the hands should be “out” for navigation and “small text” (so “out” required all text to be able to be entered with the five finger keyboard and three buttons on the mouse), and the hands should be “in” for “longer text” (paragraphs etc) using the standard keyboard.

I used to be able to use this system, so I’m trying to remember some of the interesting details. One of these was that “command accept” <A> was the far right button on the mouse. This left five buttons for chords with the left hand, and the left two buttons on the mouse for “shifts”.

The “no-shift” default was for commands to the system. So “move word” from one place to another was done as:

MW <point and click> <point and click> <A>

This is a procedural syntax, is thus modey, and requires an explicit <do it> to terminate (an “object syntax” would select first and drag the word and not need the rest). One of the reasons they stayed with this was that the analog nature of the underlying displays was “drifty” (they used small electrostatic CRTs for better quality with an 875 line TV camera strapped onto the front to blow the image up to a reasonable size — this was called “Mexican scan conversion” back then — now non-PC — it worked well enough).

Telling the system what you were trying to point at greatly helped the locator algorithms to find targets in its drifty displays.

Learning the system was kinesthetic, and took about 10–20 hours over a few days to internalize. For example, at the start it wasn’t about learning the chord for “M” or “W”, but the muscular motion for “Move Word”. At first when there was an opportunity to type, one would go to the keyboard — but very soon one would just try the chord keyboard — etc. Fluent users could type up to about 30 words a minute with “hands out”.

In practical use, this scheme worked pretty well — much of the time was spent with “hands out” navigating, typing “small things”, etc. and the response of the system was sub-second, which encouraged one to get expert. The chord keyboard and two left mouse buttons collected “downs” and sent them as a 7 bit character when all went back “up”. This worked well. The experience was like low level flying at high speed.

Note, that the initial ramp is a steep learning curve, but in a week or so you wind up with a “violin” rather than a “kazoo”. The system didn’t have anything built in to help beginners (it was an experimental system, and they were writing code for expert use). It could have been learned by children via a game interface, but that was never done.

One of the plans at Parc ca 1971 was to “do NLS on a network of minicomputers” — and there were several notions of how to do this. For example, every Alto came with a three button mouse and a five finger keyboard.

The Parc Alto with chord keyboard and 3 button mouse

Bill Duvall did a terrific subset of NLS on a Nova 800 with Parc’s experimental display HW, and it rocked. He later did an Alto version when the Altos started to become available. Larry Tesler also used the chord keyboard — not in the way NLS did — for his word processor experiments.

However, there was never a complete — really useful — system done at Parc that made central use of the chord keyboard, even though it was an excellent idea. You had to learn it to use NLS at SRI but you didn’t have to use it for the most used systems at Parc — so it didn’t get deeply incorporated into any of the day to day Parc systems. One of the reasons was that quite a lot of the UI research and design at Parc was concerned with general novice end-users, and not with experts who would have explicit training as part of their introduction to the system.

It’s worth noting that text entry on an iPhone is not a good way to do it for expert use — so we are given a novice scheme, that — ironically — the end-users then put many many hours into optimizing (but optimizing a bad scheme almost never gives you a good scheme — what you get is a slightly faster version of the bad scheme).

This is a quite general phenomenon — and is found in easy start up musical instruments (like guitars, etc.). Many “pretty good” guitar players retain poor technique that has been optimized (for example, playing lines without the pinky on the left hand, and never including the pinky as they get better — at some point this creates enormous barriers for further progress).

We find it in many school subjects, where the early versions are presented so badly that what is needed later seems like an entirely new subject (a good example is that “algebra” is really a kind of arithmetic that focuses on what “=” really implies — but for most kids it seems like something they have never seen before).

It is not unfair to point out that “marketing people” do not like to sell anything that has a real learning curve — and this has gotten even more restrictive over the years. If we extend that idea to schooling (most teachers and educational institutions don’t like to teach subjects that have real learning curves), then we can see why so many children and adults are “in deep stew” today …

## How valuable is it to apply concepts like the Curry-Howard correspondence (proofs as programs) and inductive proofs to the development of dynamic/complex systems, considering their correlation with type systems?

*https://www.quora.com/How-valuable-is-it-to-apply-concepts-like-the-Curry-Howard-correspondence-proofs-as-programs-and-inductive-proofs-to-the-development-of-dynamic-complex-systems-considering-their-correlation-with-type-systems/answer/Alan-Kay-11*

One of Marvin Minsky’s many thought provoking sayings was “The trouble with ‘New Math’ is that you have to understand it every time you use it!”. (Meaning, there is an important pragmatic place for mentally caching “rules that work” rather than working through the reasons for every use. Both are important, and some separation helps.)

Also, I will admit to a prejudice against trying to align multiple languages with multiple ways to assign meanings (this was — and is still — a big problem with formal proofs of regular programming languages).

So, I’d argue for trying to design single languages that can serve the dual purpose of being “good to program in” *and* that automatically try to verify the intentions of the programmer.

I think this is a really interesting and important problem for computerists to work on. If we think in older terms — the spectrum between assembly/C type languages and Lisp/FP type languages — the latter work better, but I think in the end are too “pristine” and not very good at systems — and the former are not expressive enough and are full of pitfalls.

Some form of “real AI” is likely to be too annoying to really help, but it’s hard to imagine pulling off the goals here without an expert system of some kind to help.

Going way back, Ivan Sutherland’s Sketchpad continuously showed you the consequences of the intentions you expressed. A lot of the time, this would lead to finding the requirements you were trying to express, winding up with what you wanted. But *some of the time* it would lead to guessing and superstitions and “poking at your system with a stick”.

An interesting wrinkle here is that Sketchpad partially succeeded by including the idea of “engineering/scientific *tolerance*” — its inferences were not exact, but the processes were set up to minimize global error measurements. This allowed it to have inherently non-linear relationships, etc.

So: an extremely important “Grand Challenge” for (real) Computer Science and (real) computer scientists!

## What is the importance of Christopher Alexander’s work for system/software designers?

*https://www.quora.com/What-is-the-importance-of-Christopher-Alexander-s-work-for-system-software-designers/answer/Alan-Kay-11*

I think the most useful of the Alexander books is the first one “Notes on a Synthesis of Form”. It was his PhD thesis at Harvard, and has thought provoking discussions of *systems* and *design*.

I don’t think his books are useful as direct guides to how to go about things in computing — and that the popular “Pattern Language” books are a bit misleading when attempts are made to apply them to computing.

In NOASOF, his main example was to try to design a new village in India by gathering many hundreds of constraints of all kinds — physical, biological, social, aesthetic, etc. — and see how to wind up with a coherent design. This thought process — including ideas in the book that work well (and those which don’t) — is invaluable for computerists to go through.

Worth the effort.

Petre Dămoc asked such a good question as a comment that I’m copying it here:

What about his magnum opus (Nature of Order)? Especially the 15 principles described in Book One. 

My intuition is telling me that these principles are extremely important for interaction design.

My reply was:

I should have mentioned these four books. IMO the best part of these books are very like the best parts of NOASOF — extremely valuable to motivate one’s own pondering.

I think of them in the same vein as I do Julian Jaynes’ “The origin of consciousness in the breakdown of the bicameral mind” — i.e. probably “not ‘true’ “, but invaluable for provoking thought.

My advice here is to take the *forms* of these thought provoking books and — instead of following the contents — make up new principles to see how the idea space can be covered (and it’s certainly OK to use some from the ideas of others).

My favorite modern “computery thinker” is Bret Victor — partly for his ideas per se, but also that he has been able to use what was valuable from the past, yet to recast the past in the light of where we are right now and his own high quality instincts, to indicate how we should be probing into the future. I don’t think that Bret has missed much that is valuable, but what he does is still “New” (rather than incremental “News”).

Prompted by a comment of Ali Krgn, here is an overall observation:

Architecture is definitely a good source of analogies for other subjects, including computing. However, I very much prefer “comfortable surroundings” to “comfortable ideas” (I’d rather be around “uncomfortable ideas” much of the time, but would not like this much in my surroundings). This is why I take C. Alexander with grains of salt — too much analogy can start missing the main points by miles.

## How much RAM did computers typically have when you first started using them?

*https://www.quora.com/How-much-RAM-did-computers-typically-have-when-you-first-started-using-them/answer/Alan-Kay-11*

I realize that I didn’t completely answer this question. I’ve now split it into 2 parts: [1] my personal experience in 1962, and [2] the more general state of things in the US at that time.

[1]

The first real computer that I programmed as a job was the IBM 1401 in 1962. It had 8K* 6-bit characters (each character had a 7th “word bit”).

* because it was a decimal machine, 8K meant 8,000 not 8192 …

I have written elsewhere on Quora about the 1401— but Quora search is “kind of abysmal”. I have answered less than 700 questions, and one would think that I (or you) should easily be able to search them …).

However, until I locate these **, here is the Wikipedia article. It is pretty informative, but lacks:

(a) that the 1401 was originally an “outlaw project” done in a back room, then grudgingly sold, then becoming spectacularly successful,

(b) our experiences (and meta experiences) with a small one in the US Air Force Air Training Command computer center in the early 60s,

(c) mentioning at least one truly significant work of meta software *** done on the 1401.

** Thanks to Mark Cleary here is one of my previous Quora answers about the 1401:

*** One of the wonderful “meta things” done on the 1401 was Val Schorre’s 1964 “Meta II” system at UCLA, a compiler-compiler that would run in an 8K 1401. I wish I had known about this when I was a 1401er, but its invention happened after I went back to school. It will be very worth any computerists’ time to read this short but loaded with information paper from 1964.

Meta II was a very clever way to use recursive procedures to parse grammars that were complex enough to describe programming languages and to emit translated code on the fly. The paper includes Meta II in itself (all in just a few lines), two complete examples of algebraic type languages, and a complete description of the virtual computer you need to make to run the examples.

If I’m not mistaken, I recall that Val’s 1401 at UCLA also only had 8K characters.

Doug Engelbart’s “Mother of all Demos” was programmed in a language — MOL — that was generated by a variant of Meta II (called “Tree Meta’).

[2]

A typical “scientific” computer ca 1962 was the IBM 7090. I’ll quote from the Wikipedia article:

The first 7090 installation was in December 1959.[1] In 1960, a typical system sold for $2.9 million (equivalent to $23 million in 2023) or could be rented for $63,500 a month (equivalent to $501,000 in 2023).

The 7090 uses a 36-bit word length, with an address space of 32,768 words (15-bit addresses).[2] It operates with a basic memory cycle of 2.18 μs, using the IBM 7302 Core Storage core memory technology from the IBM 7030 (Stretch) project.

I never wound up having to program the 7090/4 series. But it could be fun here to compare it with its biggest competitor at that time: the Control Data 3600, designed by Seymour Cray.

A typical system sold for $1,200,000 ($9.5M today — so less than half the IBM 7094), was a 48 bit machine (and could have a max memory of 256K words), and was a bit faster.

I wrote quite a few programs for this at the National Center for Atmospheric Reseach in Boulder, starting in 1963. IBM called Control Data “Brand X” (possibly because it was so good they didn’t want to even mention the name).

This was developed into a whole line of 3000 series machines, and CDC made a lot of money during this time period.

## What is the origin of the name "The Internet"? Was it chosen as a play on words with "interconnected networks"? Were there any other names considered before "The Internet" was chosen?

*https://www.quora.com/What-is-the-origin-of-the-name-The-Internet-Was-it-chosen-as-a-play-on-words-with-interconnected-networks-Were-there-any-other-names-considered-before-The-Internet-was-chosen/answer/Alan-Kay-11*

JCR Licklider — an experimental psychologist and (ca 1959/60s) fan of interactive computing — was given a lot of money by the DoD to set up a long range computer research community. One of his first memos looked like this:

There is a good story (I’ve told it elsewhere in Quora) about why he called it this.

The first pass at this was a large experiment in packet-switching: the ARPAnet. This was instigated by a successor of “Lick” — Bob Taylor — and made to happen by Larry Roberts.

What should be done next was pretty unanimous, and was started by Larry Roberts. It was generally called “Inter-networking”. You can guess what this was shortened to eventually.

Xerox Parc actually had a working inter-networking system that spanned the US before the official Internet — it was called “PUP” — for “Parc Universal Packets” — and Parc researchers were part of the larger Internet design committee whose main force was Vint Cerf (but which was a truly amazing group effort of top designers who wanted to work with each other).

I would give Steve Crocker the main credit for the way the networking research community was organized — and so would Vint (this came up when we had dinner a few weeks ago).

Looking at some of the other answers has prompted me to say a bit more here. The ARPA community did not regard the ARPAnet — which sent its first packets in 1969 — as an “internetworking” scheme. But, as mentioned above, the desire/plan to develop internetworking was already in the air.

Both Bob Kahn and Vint Cerf worked on the ARPAnet, and in the early 70s started to produce proposal versions of what was to become TCP/IP.

Thanks to Steve Crocker and the way the network design process was set up within ARPA, there are a series of “Requests for Comment” documents that provide a wonderful history of the ideas. (“Request For Comment” was thought to be less aggressive and more friendly than “Requests For Proposals” that were the norm in DoD.)

The Ethernet was done at Parc ca 1973 to connect computing resources there, and very quickly some of the Altos were programmed to be what we would call “routers” today, and were used to internetwork Ethernets, the ARPAnet, etc. The protocols were called “PUP” (as mentioned above).

There is also a somewhat funny story told by others and myself about how the first wireless use of the ARPAnet (using an old Ford bread truck full of gear) was used to transmit reports to Washington DC from one of Palo Alto’s outdoor beer gardens. This was soon used to connect to Don Davies’ packet network at the National Physical Labs in the UK. Here’s a talk I did that summarises a fair amount of the work back then:

## How would Alan Kay go about designing a systems design course? What contents should be covered, and what knowledge or skills should one gain? Which exemplary projects/papers should be included to facilitate understanding?

*https://www.quora.com/How-would-Alan-Kay-go-about-designing-a-systems-design-course-What-contents-should-be-covered-and-what-knowledge-or-skills-should-one-gain-Which-exemplary-projects-papers-should-be-included-to-facilitate/answer/Alan-Kay-11*

In the true fashion of the 1960s-thru-1970s ARPA-IPTO research community (which included Parc), I would try to find the best people who could do this, and help find funds to support them.

I would try to help form a joint vision large and comprehensive enough to excite and guide.

Compared to what I think is needed, there would only be a few ideas that I could help with (and I think most of the central people we’d get as PIs would already have them).

One big notion and set of questions would be how to go about helping all of us — especially the students — internalize a much better “systems consciousness” (i.e. better “feelings” and “guesses” about systems, etc.).

I started to “think systems” from getting a degree in molecular biology, and first being fascinated by what was called “Embryology” back then (now “Morphogenesis”), then Biochemistry, and then when Watson’s great book “Molecular Biology of the Gene” appeared in 1965. At the time I was working my way through college as a programmer of super computers of the day for the National Center For Weather research — I didn’t know anything important about computing or computing systems, and there was some, but little, overlap with the weather models and computer systems, and systems in general.

Today, there are a variety of ways to use computers to get started on “thinking systems” — especially in both cognitive and visceral ways. I don’t think I know all of them at this point. There are “massively parallel simulators” (like StarLogo, etc.) in which it is easy to set up simple conditions that generate complex non-linear behaviors.

The Apple “Vivarium” Project was aimed at helping children learn to make and view the world via “systems glasses”.

There is Bret Victor’s Dynamicland which creates a wondeful system’s world in which one is embedded and can influence in easy and highly influential ways. I would definitely try to create early experiences and projects of many kinds using this kind of media.

One of many threads running though these ideas would try to help learners transition from normal commonsense (and wrong and weak) notions of static stabilities to the large idea that any stabilities are actually *dynamic stabilities*, and thus processes of some kind are necessary to keep desirable propertes within tolerances, etc.

And then there is *scaling* …

And then there is …

Etc.

Basically (I think) there are many things that would be good to do and learn before computer systems themselves become the object of study. Since much of the early ideas would also be reified using computer systems, being able to later “pop the hatches” of these could be a great start, etc.

There would be much more to this — and far beyond the scope of Quora (and my personal scope). I should have added at the beginning that I would normally think about this for months before proffering ideas — but the fun (and pitfall) of Quora is to see what can be done as a single stream of response.

It would be a great “grand challenge” project!

## What is Alan Kay's perspective on the obsession with learning memory management and other "low-level" aspects when it comes to programming education?

*https://www.quora.com/What-is-Alan-Kays-perspective-on-the-obsession-with-learning-memory-management-and-other-low-level-aspects-when-it-comes-to-programming-education/answer/Alan-Kay-11*

I react to this question in the way I react to questions that are essentially about “how much of a subset of something important can we isolate as separate teachable subject before we destroy the connection to the “something important”?”

For example, to what extent can you isolate “reading and writing” and even “literature” from *ideas*?

It is not unlikely that most educational systems in the world do just such a separation — and, if so, I don’t agree with it at all.

Programming is often quite isolated from systems design (and from systems themselves) because it is often taught in isolation as “data structures and procedures and algorithms”. I think this is quite a bad approach. (And systems are not the only larger ideas that need to be understood and heeded e.g. integrity and “before the ‘fact’ engineering” *)

The question before us falls into the really interesting category of “runnable math” — meaning that we’d like to think of most programming and systems design in terms of their “relational requirements” rather than what is often needed to convert these into runnable and usable systems.

I’m old enough to have been brought up in a mathematical, scientific, and engineering world in which part of the years of learning were spent on really understanding and being able to use fundamental principles and materials both when needed and to ground any higher levels of understanding.

My prejudice is definitely that this is still a very good — imperative — idea. It is still being done in the established fields of maths, sciences, and engineering.

However, there have been explosions of knowledge in many fields — including computing — so it is definitely worth pondering how to allocate our learning time to trying to understand much larger fields.

I have written a few Quora answers praising the Nissan and Schocken “from nothing to an interesting program” approach.

These days I think I would try to work with them to take a second pass at this wonderful work they’ve done. (This stuff can’t be praised too highly, but I think an even larger perspective and a fresh pass would yield great dividends.) For example, the approach to the HW could be made a fair amount simpler without losing an rigor, and the goals for the SW part could be greatly expanded without requiring more than a bit more total bulk of code.

That would be a really interesting project, and also a good way of answering the slightly different and larger question that could have been asked here. I.e. say “Yes” via radically changing what it means to “learn to program”.

* “before the ‘fact’ engineering” is a phrase coined by Margaret Hamilton, who was head of Apollo Guidance Computer mission SW (everything thing except for the OS). The ‘fact’ referred to any kind of errors, especially crashes. The idea was that the engineering’s main goal was to prevent ‘facts’ from happening during a mission.

The evidence is that there was never a SW failure over all the Apollo missions, despite the enormous limitations of both the HW and SW media they were required to use.

## What do you think is the future of software engineering? Could advancements in technology eventually render it obsolete, or will these advancements serve as valuable tools that enhance the work of software engineers rather than replacing them?

*https://www.quora.com/What-do-you-think-is-the-future-of-software-engineering-Could-advancements-in-technology-eventually-render-it-obsolete-or-will-these-advancements-serve-as-valuable-tools-that-enhance-the-work-of-software-engineers/answer/Alan-Kay-11*

Here’s part of a slide I used in a talk in 2021 expressing a kind of “Hippocratic Oath” within Engineering:

The first two have been around for thousands of years. The ones for airplanes and software more recently. It’s worth noting that in every era there have been people — sometimes even engineers — who are willing to bypass these for various forms of gain and/or convenience.

There is also the problem that only parts of “Software Engineering” resemble “Established Engineering” — much of what is called “SE” is considerably more ad hoc than the term demands.

An historical perspective on Engineering will reveal many changes in what pro-level engineers in each era do, and what kinds of tools they learn and use. However, the “Do no harm” ethic has been quite constant over time.

We also have to take note of the deep human trait of *normalizing* what is generally going on in each present time. For example, it is big news when a plane crashes and kills several hundred on board, but in the US in 2022 there was an average of 116 traffic deaths a day from vehicle crashes alone. Much worse, there is an average of 1315 deaths per day from smoking. This is not only *not* front page news, it is not even reported in most news media.

This means that a deep danger in the future of engineering would be a “normalization creep” downwards to levels of harm not considered acceptable today. We can see hints of this in many parts of computing, especially “social” media and so-called “AI”. These are quite dangerous and harmful in their current form, but most of the population, including the engineers involved, have normalized that causing harm in this and other ways is quite acceptable. (And, of course, we can see many other examples of technologies invented and produced via engineering that are gradually turning the planet uninhabitable.)

Another deep human trait is to try to avoid paying the full cost of most things, and especially to try to amortize costs not just to the future, but to future generations. For example, most infrastructure objects — such as bridges — are costed for constructing them, but not to replace them or do major maintenance 50 years or so hence. The software industries have taken up this unfortunate behavior all too whole-heartedly.

We also have to note that the level of expression that is used to create software has not changed much since the 80s — and that this is in great contrast to the progression of levels of language that happened in the late 50s to the late 70s. Meanwhile, “Moore’s Law” at the components level continued exponentially, and without languages/development environments, approaches, etc. keeping pace (and not even keeping pace with the development and use of tools in the more established engineering disciplines — ironically using computers for CAD and SIM in ways that the computing field itself shunned).

My guess is that the two main culprits were (a) rampant commercialization starting in the 80s, and (b) the lack of “level of skills” and ways to determine these that were analogous to the medical and established engineering professions.

When Facebook took itself off the Internet for a day a few years ago (including its own offices), I started poking around to see what led to this. I found that Facebook essentially does “unit tests” via thousands of configuration checking programs whenever a change is made. There was not a test that would say “you must not partition the Internet on purpose”, etc.

Note that trying to write thousands of individual laws that together capture the larger intent of a process doesn’t scale, and in the end is a terrible approach. This is similar to the Boeing 737 Max autopilot — which also had thousands of “laws” and responses. However, they didn’t have what John McCarthy called “commonsense” knowledge that most humans use to bridge between the specific and the general. Facebook code didn’t have any sense that the larger goal was to be on the Internet 24/7, and the autopilot didn’t know that it had people to protect and that diving towards the ground to correct a stall at low altitude is not to be done.

What is quite sad here is that Moore’s Law did come through with the kind of scaling needed to handle these larger issues. But the ideals and perspective for what “real AI” (and “real programming in the 21st century) need got lost when a subset of the “real AI” problem (fuzzy useful correlations with little meaning) replaced “real AI”.

——— added June 19 2024 ———

Here’s something recently, very dangerous, and to this point:

Yikes!

I reckon that we’ve now lost almost 40 years of needed development of “higher level expression with integrity of meaning”. Doug Lenat’s CYC system had many of the right ideas, but needed to be redone a few times to reflect learning curve effects on how the architecture should work.

Here’s one way to think about what is needed. It has analogies to classical engineering, but is of much larger scope. It also has analogies to “societal engineering” but constitutes a very large step from where we are.

The center of what is needed is a set of processes that can represent most of the important meanings and goals in our century, and to be able to do it in ways that the validations of meanings can be understandable to we humans. Engineering has done this with various kinds of standards, including physical ones that represent the meanings of core concepts. Some societies have done this with carefully written relatively small constitutions, against which specific laws and actions can be tested. (Note that there are too many degrees of freedom for “case law”, so determining “legality” almost certainly has to be done dynamically.)

To my mind — maybe it is now just the mind of an old fogey — this returns us to many of the ideals and visions of the early 60s. This time around, there are enough resources to do a much more complete job at “Software Engineering with Meaning and Safety”. (It won’t look much like what is called Software Engineering today, but that is much of the point here!)

## I’m currently a teenager and I started looking at philosophy. I want to start taking a dive into it but I don’t know where to start. Any certain topics or books that I should look into?

*https://www.quora.com/I-m-currently-a-teenager-and-I-started-looking-at-philosophy-I-want-to-start-taking-a-dive-into-it-but-I-don-t-know-where-to-start-Any-certain-topics-or-books-that-I-should-look-into/answer/Alan-Kay-11*

A good and somewhat tricky question …

First, what does *philosophy* mean to you?

I think of it as the kind of deep thinking that one has to learn to do when science, etc., no longer serves — but you will have your own slant on this. The underlying notions of science will still help thinking about issues that don’t lend themselves to empirical experiments.

The contrast between maths and science can also help provide some grounding to the use of logic and representations in language. Einstein pointed out to fellow physicists in 1921:

“As far as the laws of mathematics refer to reality, they are not certain;

 and as far as they are certain, they do not refer to reality.”

The larger meaning of this is that reasoning in language can express “certainty” but this is only about the logical entailment of the conclusion, not about “the world outside our heads”.

Another path to be negotiated is the one between learning what others have thought in the past (and are now thinking) and the central point here of learning to think your own thoughts in deeper and more fruitful ways. You will need to build up a lot of both.

One way to do this is to note down *questions* as you read the ideas of others (this is better in the long run than e.g. simply underlining and learning the ideas of others).

It will help you (a lot) to write down your current *burning questions*

I like “carpet bombing reading”, but sometimes a single “slim volume” can be a good way to get started. A good one — by Thomas Nagel — is “What Does It All Mean?”. You will find Nagel’s approach to getting into philosophy similar to what I’ve been advocating — I particularly like the introduction of this book: to me, it is the essence of how to start thinking about “difficult stuff”.

A few generations ago, Bertrand Russell wrote quite a few books for the general public about ideas, and presented them in a genial good natured but not trivial way. His book “The problems of philosophy” could be a good start.

In any case, the first cousin of philosophy is bullshit. This is both useful and a snare. The trick is to use bullshit to speculate, but then not to get caught in your own waste products! (e.g. by believing the bullshit). As with the invention of science, finding other ways to deal with ideas other than simply “believing” them is the key to making real progress.

Good luck, and have fun!

## Can you provide some examples of a "thinking machine" that existed before computers were invented?

*https://www.quora.com/Can-you-provide-some-examples-of-a-thinking-machine-that-existed-before-computers-were-invented/answer/Alan-Kay-11*

LexisNexis defines “machine” as

A machine is any system structure that can be used to complete a task by utilizing energy.

Lewis Mumford used the term “megamachines” as part of his approach for understanding and analysing societies — and pointed out that most societies were in fact “megamachines”.

“Artificial” — according to the Oxford English Dictionary — means:

made or produced by human beings rather than occurring naturally, especially as a copy of something natural.

With all this in mind, let me propose *modern science* as not only a “thinking machine” and an “artifical intelligence”, but as the most powerful and successful manifestations of these ideas so far, and in history.

I think this is not only quite lost on most of today’s computerists who work on so-called “AI” (which is even very far from the original definitions and larger understandings of the original founders).

For example, one of the keystones of “real science” is not only that *internal deductions and inductions are insufficient for doing science* but that the whole enterprise — including empirical observations and studies — are extremely difficult in general, and for the human mind in particular.

This is partly because — as Francis Bacon pointed out 400+ years ago — the human race is not set up for thinking clearly (a) genetically (b) culturally (c) linguistically (d) academically. “Scientia” back then meant “gathering of knowledge”, but Bacon pointed out that the results of the four “idols” above that humans “worshipped” led to the “gathering of distorted and quite wrong ‘knowledge’ “, and that what would very well help matters would be to invent a “new science”: new methods and new organizations that could partly get around our biased brain/minds, cultures, languages, and teaching.

What we call “real science” today is the “new science” that Bacon called for.

There are too many facets of “real science” for the size of a Quora answer, but let me point out that “real science” requires a society of scientists who are willing not just to explore in new ways but to test out the ideas in new and tougher ways (since most humans have “confirmation bias” which makes it difficult for the formulators of theories to test them deeply enough (so other scientists often do a better job of testing, etc.)).

(Note that funders often have considerable confirmation bias, etc.)

If any attempts are made to “do AI on a computer”, they should take into account what “real science” has found it necessary to do to generate necessary levels of confidence in the results. Without this we have a combination of confabulation with credulity — often associated with belief systems, such as religion — that has been really dangerous over history, and especially dangerous today.

## What would be the place of AI in Doug Engelbart's vision of 'Augmenting Human Intellect'? How can we reconsider things within current AI 'developments'?

*https://www.quora.com/What-would-be-the-place-of-AI-in-Doug-Engelbarts-vision-of-Augmenting-Human-Intellect-How-can-we-reconsider-things-within-current-AI-developments/answer/Alan-Kay-11*

It’s very worthwhile to read Doug’s original plan in 1962. They could only work on a subset of this, and ca 1970 they wound up being identified with the subset (this often happens).

Find this version of the plan on Engelbart’s website (hint: type “Engelbart” into Google).

Below is the summary of the large scale plan. You can see in the red box a mention of various technologies they intended to use — and in the large scale plan itself, you can read how they planned to use “AI” (you need to remember that many terms — such as “AI” — had a very different meaning in 1962 (62 years ago!) and they certainly were not thinking of such limited and counterproductive technologies called “AI” today (such as ML, LLM, etc.)).

In talks that people have posted to YouTube, I’ve explained some of the big ideas from this deep group of researchers.

One big distinction in the 1962 time period is that they thought of “machine intelligence” as being a kind of complimentary set of thinking tools that could be “symbiotic” to how humans were able to think. They were not at all thinking about something like a slave or a major domo, but something more like a research assistant or a “Memex” (the latter was a big influence on Doug’s thinking).

In the very late 60s the “official AI researchers” started to think that something like “intelligent Greek slaves” were needed for the “Romans” (Americans), and became rivals to Doug’s notion of elevating human thinking rather than just elevating power. This was a bad idea then … and it’s a bad idea today.

For completeness, here are the references for this 1962 plan. Also, Ivan Sutherland and his work on Sketchpad are mentioned in this document, but there was no reference because Ivan wrote his thesis in Jan 1963.

## Why are object-oriented classes named classes? What is the etymology of object- oriented classes?

*https://www.quora.com/Why-are-object-oriented-classes-named-classes-What-is-the-etymology-of-object-oriented-classes/answer/Alan-Kay-11*

The second version of Simula (Simula-67) used the term “Class” for the descriptions that could be instantiated into “objects” which carried out the descriptions. Some of the background for this term very likely came from its use in mathematics.

The history has some points of interest. For example, the first version of Simula (Simula I) used the term “Activity” for the descriptions that could be instantiated into “Processes” which carried out the descriptions. Ivan Sutherland’s Sketchpad system predated Simula, and used the term “Master” for the descriptions that could be instantiated into “instances” which carried out the descriptions.

Other terms for “that description which can be instantiated” have been used over the years. For example, note that the “Processes” in multi-processing/time-sharing OSs are actually instances of a special kind of restricted virtual machine which the OSs supports and protects.

It is also worth noting that in both Simulas the description (class/activity) is not an object. A language in which every description is an actual object — e.g. Smalltalk — turned out to be a very useful idea.

## How can I convince myself that “real OOP” is a better way to build systems? What’s the reason other than Alan Kay’s “god-given vision” — Is there any math behind these ideas or are they just a bunch of “good-looking” ideas with "cool" rhetoric?

*https://www.quora.com/How-can-I-convince-myself-that-real-OOP-is-a-better-way-to-build-systems-What-s-the-reason-other-than-Alan-Kay-s-god-given-vision-Is-there-any-math-behind-these-ideas-or-are-they-just-a-bunch-of-good-looking-ideas/answer/Alan-Kay-11*

“Interesting” question, and “way to phrase it”.

First, I doubt there was any “god” behind my “vision”. And why would “math” make you feel any better if you are asking about “better ways to build systems”? (That is the province of engineering, which only part of the time can use math to help, and sometimes has to get by “workable heuristics”.)

And then, a key question is whether my almost 60 year old vision holds today after factors of a few millions of Moore’s Law?

I always start off by doubting “things held to be true” in order to help thinking. And I certainly think that what I thought in 1966 should be suspect in 2024.

The basic idea was that a really simple way to think about systems — that was already in use — was the analytic idea of identifying subparts and the communications between them. My little idea was that this could be modeled as “little complete computers” on a “network” communicating by “messages”, and this could be “mathematically neat and complete” if every entity (including the parts, network and messages) was in the form of “little complete computers”.

The ancillary observation was that this would take a lot of software and hardware engineering to be made practical enough to work.

This is what I called “OOP” back then.

Trying to look at today, I think the ways of trying to understand systems by decomposition and build them by synthesizing organizations of parts are still the main ones (and are still problematical — but likely to still be needed and useful).

However, I think the practical tools for understanding and making systems have not kept up with the immense scalings that have happened over the last 60 years or so. (Something worth pondering is that a qualitative scaling should also provide more computing power for better ways to intercommunicate, and thus better ways to “send and receive messages” — and this means much better ways to decompose problems and model better solutions.

Depending on what you think “Real OOP” means might help your first question. If you think it means “the way we (Parc) e.g. built systems in the 70s”, then only a few of those principles still hold, and better ways are needed. If you think what “Real OOP” should mean (in this day and age), then I think you need to help invent the practical forms of *what is actually needed* today.

I think it will be hard to actually understand any complex thing without *modularization” of some kind (and this will require techniques for “intermodule communication and coordination”).

It’s up to you to decide whether what I thought about 60 years ago has any bearing on this today, and whether it was a kind of “applied algebraics and logic to practical problems” (along the lines of how John McCarthy thought about things).

## It has been said that Windows is Bill Gates way of helping Seagate to sell ever larger hard disk drives. If that is true, then I claim that Smalltalk is Alan Kay's way of helping Intel sell ever more computationally capacious microprocessor chips?

*https://www.quora.com/It-has-been-said-that-Windows-is-Bill-Gates-way-of-helping-Seagate-to-sell-ever-larger-hard-disk-drives-If-that-is-true-then-I-claim-that-Smalltalk-is-Alan-Kays-way-of-helping-Intel-sell-ever-more-computationally/answer/Alan-Kay-11*

First, let me copy the OP’s answer to his own question:

Bill Buckley:

The problem with this post, which I placed, has much to do with Quora’s limit on question size. So, I will try again. Dr. Kay, is it unreasonable for me to have said in my Graduate Seminar course (for the MS Computer Science), “It has been said that Windows is Bill Gates way of helping Seagate to sell ever larger hard disk drives. If that is true, then I claim that Smalltalk is Alan Kay’s way of helping Intel to sell ever more computationally capacious mircroprocessor chips?”

The top question is complex linguistically. The first sentence looks to be a “proverbial metaphor”, but the next phrase is “If that is true …”.

It isn’t “true”, so the rest of the question — a deduction — doesn’t follow as the writer would wish (of course, implications don’t require their preconditions, but normal usage is “if and only if” and these do).

Now to address Bill Buckley’s comment.

I would offer that “yes, it was unreasonable for you to say that”. The largest reason is that I never was interested in helping Intel do anything but start to create “emulation processors” for dealing with a variety of very high level languages (e.g. much higher in expressive power and safety than C) that both existed and needed to be invented.

I viewed Smalltalk as “something good in its timeframe and scaling”, to be superceded as soon as possible.

The opposite of my aims actually happened: (a) Intel stayed with extremely poor architectures and tried to make them faster, but not better, (b) Smalltalk did not get materially/qualitatively reinvented, and is still around today in close to original form.

## What is the Chronology of Early OOP? (see self-answer for details)

*https://www.quora.com/What-is-the-Chronology-of-Early-OOP-see-self-answer-for-details/answer/Alan-Kay-11*

There’s “early” and “Really Early”.

“Really Early” mostly happened in the 60s (with a little continuity back into the 50s).

My best recollections are in a history I wrote that was requested in the early 90s by the ACM “The Early History Of Smalltalk”. A version of this (without the Appendices) can be found on Bret Victor’s site: The Early History Of Smalltalk

The notion of data structures containing pointers to procedures goes way back. I mention one example in this history that was in use when I started programming in 1961. Also, data structures with multiple fields were commonly called “objects” (procedure pointers or not) — so I made a bad choice in 1966 calling this new area “object oriented programming” (if conveys a poor image of the idea).

If I were to do another pass through this history, I probably would have said more about Doug Ross (whom Ivan Sutherland mentions in his 1963 thesis). Doug was an early programmer on Whirlwind in the 50s and one of the first to write digital graphical simulations (bouncing balls, etc.) that were common on analog computers (these were partly to show that Whirlwind was really fast — it was one of the earliest — maybe the first — bit parallel computers).

Two big ideas that were being thought about early on in different areas of computing were (a) “instantiation” and (b) that “meaning” had to include dynamics.

For example in the data base world there was the notion of unit records of a particular arrangement of fields (initially on punched cards). One path was eventually to the Data Division of COBOL and what led up to it (this predated scientific computing by many years e.g. Algol 60 only had numbers, strings and arrays — “records” were in the future).

WIth all due respect to Doug Ross, it was Ivan Sutherland ca 1961–2 who thought about instantiation of dynamic “objects” — this for the purpose of creating what is arguably the first real interactive graphics language and system: Sketchpad.

Just as interesting, and a tad earlier, we have Bob Barton describing the architecture of the Burroughs B5000 — which also was the first to have its OS completely written in a High Level Language (initially an extension of Algol 58, then Algol 60 (called ESPOL): A New Approach To The Functional Design Of A Digital Computer.

In this case the *hardware* was more higher level than any of the languages of the day — it could be thought of as a “Simula I” machine but before Simula. It included both instantiation and “meanings as including dynamics”, etc.

Instantiation from a “Master” (Sketchpad term) or an “Activity” (Simula I) term (both of which are now called “Class” (from the later Simula 67), does not require inheritance chains to be extremely useful. The “Master” establishes a *category* that defines generically how the instances should behave and appear. Sketchpad allowed Masters to be made from any *composition* of instances, and this was very powerful.

As the Smalltalk history explains, a lot of early ideas about “processes” were combined into a single definitional idea for a new way to think about “objects”. Some of these additional ideas included the kinds of instantiation into “virtual machines” that multi-process and time-sharing OSs were starting to do — this is a great way to start thinking about the ideas, but the overheads in having processes be “large” had to be eliminated.

Pure math — in “algebras” etc — uses ideas that are like “inheritance” to get both power and logical coherency — so the notion of “inheritance” appeared early (e.g. in Simula 67).

I think I explained in the Smalltalk history that the Lispish late-binding approach taken by Smalltalk-72 allowed many different inheritance schemes to be explored (including the very useful “slot inheritance” adopted in some of the AI systems of the day (e.g. Pat Winston’s thesis).

The original plan for the Alto computer at Xerox Parc was to replace it with a much faster one in a few years to take advantage of Moore’s Law, etc. However, Xerox did not want to pay for many new machines (they were already complaining about the 100s of Altos we were making). This put a huge squeeze on researchers (like us) who were depending on HW capacity to stay very late bound.

The need for faster and larger on the same machine inspired Dan Ingalls to design Smalltalk-76, which was more of a compromise between the Lisp and Algol worlds, but was a brilliant design and not much flexibility was lost (and it was almost 200 times faster than Smalltalk-72). Part of the design was the decision to use (and be really careful with) single inheritance for the system (but to still try experiments in *what should Masters look like?*

This worked out well because we were primarily trying to invent a wide-spectrum usable form of “personal computing” rather than a programming language (and this helped all around). Smalltalk worked really well at the scales we had back then. But it was clear that e.g. “inheritance” was going to be tough to scale, and a workable multiple inheritance needed to be more than ad hoc ideas. For example, MIT’s Flavors were a perfect double-edged sword and very difficult to handle (and much larger in code than the entire Smalltalk system at Parc).

Basically: scaling really called for a “knowledge based epistemological design” that would require a lot more than just combinations of inheritance and compositions and mixins, etc. We considered this necessary, but outside the scope of our research.

## How can anyone who is intelligent believe in god?

*https://www.quora.com/How-can-anyone-who-is-intelligent-believe-in-god/answer/Alan-Kay-11*

David Moore wrote a good answer:

Once we realize that our biological brain/minds are (a) set up to remember and believe, and (b) all of this activity is internal, we can also realize that (c) what we think is “reality” is actually our own internal theatre playing back combinations of our beliefs and sometimes tiny signals from outside us. This means that we are always “dreaming” (and we hope our waking dreams are better maps of what’s going on than those while we are sleeping).

Using these terms we can see why David Moore uses the term “hallucination” — and we should also be able to see that the best science can do is to make better “maps” — “representations” — of what more careful investigations can find out.

Because scientists are humans, their brain/minds also *believe* — and good scientists will try to include the active idea of “this is a belief” as a label on their beliers.

The term “god” in the question is vague: Wikipedia declines a simple definition such as “an entity superior to human beings in many — if not all — ways”. Instead, the article loads the term with many historical perspectives, etc.

Long ago I majored in Molecular Biology — and still find it endlessly fascinating.

One conjecture that MolBio gives rise to is that it is entirely possible — using just the biology of this planet — for there to have been or be “an entity superior to human beings in many — if not all — ways”.

I think most intelligent and knowledgeable people would be able to believe in the above sentence. It is about possibilities related to well known science and weak, but reasonable definition of the term “god”.

I don’t think there is enough evidence to actually *locate* such an enitity, *or to actually believe in its existence*.

I think this would/should preclude belief in actualities for stronger definitions of “god”.

However, one of the interesting pitfalls of science is that when we are on the trail of a conjecture, it is hard to not “sort of believe in it”. And, one of the largest stumbling blocks in trying to think is “confirmation bias” — and we scientists have this problem along with everyone else.

I think “conjecture” is the twilight area for most thinkers. This is where our “waking dreams” have the most trouble (and fun). The theatrical nature of our biological mind is most of the time — a great gift — and sometimes leads us astray. Frank Thomas, the famous Disney animator, once told me that they were worried that the audience for “Snow White” would not be afraid for her when threatened by the huntsman (she was just a series of drawings). But there was no need to worry, because — in theatre — the audience can get completely emotionally involved in wooden puppets, and cry when one is “killed”.

Here’s a good one. Suppose we believe we are an atheist — and have supportive reasons into which we’ve put a lot of effort. But, how tough should we be as a member of the audience in a great play where belief in a god is the center of the driving idea? Can we give ourselves over to the play — for the sake of the play — and then come back to our main set of beliefs when the show is done?

The next night, in the very same building — also with great words being spoken and great music being played — we are now in a political rally. I don’t think we should give ourselves over to it, just because it is set up like a theatrical performance. I think we should really be skeptical and try to avoid simple believing — even — especially! — when we think we like the candidate.

The real question is where to put our story worlds. I don’t think we should try to do away with them — so much meaning is wrapped up in them. But, the advent of science shows that we can also have mental worlds — still kind of story-like, still with some believing going on — that are much clearer depictions of “what’s out there?”.

Shouldn’t we be teaching children how to live in and use their various mental worlds, rather than being trapped in them?

As stated, this feels like a “trick question”, because any Turing complete mechanism can be programmed to run any meta-circular evaluator. I feel that I’m missing something here. Am I? Please tell me more …
